sections.title: Human language and computation
Speech movements in MRI
Why speech is a remarkable learned skill

teaching.text: **Speech is a complex learned skill.** Children learn to coordinate their speech organs with little explicit instruction and very little visual feedback about what those organs are doing.
children: A child can develop a large vocabulary and near-adult language between about two and four years of age. Reading and writing whole words develop later and require much more explicit instruction.

teaching.text: **Articulatory phonetics** studies how structures in the vocal tract move to produce speech. The tongue and lips must make coordinated movements to produce different sounds.
**Speech technology** attempts to model this human ability. Understanding human speech and understanding how AI models speech are connected questions.

sections.title: Air vibration and acoustic phonetics

teaching.text: **Acoustic phonetics** studies speech sounds, including how air vibrates in the vocal tract. The vocal tract is the air passage shaped by the tongue and the surrounding structures.
children: The passage can be represented as a straight column of air to make its vibration easier to study. Straightening the drawing simplifies the shape of the model.

sections.title: Why scientific understanding of AI matters

teaching.text: **AI literacy means understanding how AI systems operate.** Knowing how to build or use a system does not necessarily explain how its behavior arises.
AI has psychological, economic, social and environmental harms, as well as potential benefits in areas such as medicine and environmental engineering.
children: Understanding these systems helps people assess their benefits and harms. This matters for scientists using AI, politicians developing rules and lawyers dealing with its consequences.

sections.title: Course goals

teaching.text: Understanding **human speech**, **basic physical principles** and **AI models of cognition** connects several kinds of knowledge. Speech can be studied as a cognitive skill, a physical process and a skill that a computer attempts to model.

**Elementary programming** develops methodical reasoning. Working across linguistics, physics, psychology, biology and computer science also develops the ability to connect ideas and use AI more thoughtfully.

sections.title: Moving from memorization to creative reasoning

teaching.text: **Diotima’s ladder** distinguishes memorization and repetition from creative understanding. **Creative reasoning** asks how ideas relate. Similar-looking things can work differently, and different-looking things can share an underlying principle.
children: Asking and answering questions develops this kind of understanding. It involves posing problems, solving them, reading critically and explaining ideas rather than only repeating them.

sections.title: Voicing and place through sustained fricatives

teaching.text: **Voicing** means whether the vocal folds vibrate. The sounds in each pair keep the same place of articulation while changing voicing.
children: The pairs are f and v, th in “thing” and th in “that,” s and z, and sh in “mesh” and the sound in “beige.” The second sound in each pair is voiced.

teaching.text: **Place of articulation** identifies where the vocal tract is narrowed. Moving from one pair to another changes that location. Voicing and place therefore describe different properties of a consonant.

sections.title: The fricative system

teaching.text: **Fricatives** are produced by sending air through a narrow opening. Their classification combines **place of articulation** with **voicing**.
children: **Labial** f and v use the lip region. **Dental** th sounds use the teeth. **Alveolar** s and z use the ridge just behind the upper teeth. **Postalveolar** sh and the sound in “beige” are produced farther back.

teaching.text: Each place has a voiceless and a voiced member. For example, f and v share their place but differ in whether the vocal folds vibrate.

sections.title: Stop place, voicing, and nasality

teaching.text: A **stop** involves a complete closure in the mouth. The place of that closure distinguishes three groups.
children: The lips close for **p, b and m**. The tongue tip closes at the alveolar ridge for **t, d and n**. The back of the tongue closes at the velum, or soft palate, for **k, g and ng**.

teaching.text: Among the **oral stops**, p, t and k are voiceless, while b, d and g are voiced. Air is released through the mouth when the closure opens.
The **nasal stops** m, n and ng keep the mouth closed while air escapes through the nose. The **velum** lowers to open that route.
children: For example, d and n are both voiced and alveolar. Their difference is the oral or nasal route taken by the air.

lecture02.title: 02 · Speech structure and learning in AI

sections.title: Human language and technology
Lecture agenda
Internal coordination during speech
Fricative place and voicing

teaching.text: **Fricatives** use a narrow opening in the vocal tract. The **place of articulation** identifies the location of that opening, while **voicing** identifies whether the vocal folds vibrate.
children: The labial pair is f and v. The dental pair is th in “thing” and th in “that.” The alveolar pair is s and z. The postalveolar pair is sh and the sound in “beige.”

teaching.text: Within each pair, the place stays the same and voicing changes. Comparing f with s changes place instead.

sections.title: Oral and nasal stop comparisons

teaching.text: A **stop** has a complete closure in the mouth. The lips produce p, b and m. The tongue tip at the alveolar ridge produces t, d and n. The tongue back at the velum produces k, g and ng.
**Oral stops** release the air through the mouth. The voiceless oral stops are p, t and k, and the voiced oral stops are b, d and g.
children: For **nasal stops**, the velum lowers so air can leave through the nose while the mouth stays closed. These are m, n and ng.

sections.title: Three dimensions of consonant knowledge

teaching.text: Consonants are organized by **voicing**, **place of articulation** and **manner of articulation**. Voicing concerns vocal-fold vibration, place concerns where the mouth is narrowed or closed, and manner concerns how air passes through.
children: **Fricatives** allow air through a narrow gap. **Oral stops**, also called **plosives**, close the mouth passage and release air through it. **Nasal stops** close the mouth passage while letting air leave through the nose.

teaching.text: The table combines these properties. **D and n** are both voiced and alveolar, but d is an oral stop and n is a nasal stop.
children: English nasal stops are voiced. Recognizing this organization shows how much structured knowledge is involved in producing ordinary consonants.

sections.title: AI as a model of psychological abilities

teaching.text: **Artificial intelligence, or AI, models psychological abilities** such as knowing, recognizing, attending, acting and learning. These are abilities found in animals, including humans.
Ideas about human behavior and cognition contribute to AI design. AI therefore has connections to the study of minds and brains, as well as to computing.

sections.title: Taylor’s cloze procedure

teaching.text: The **cloze procedure** tests completion. Words are removed from a passage, and a reader supplies the missing words.
children: The procedure was developed to measure readability. Completing a passage requires using the words that remain to work out what belongs in the gaps.

sections.title: Closure turns incomplete input into a whole pattern

teaching.text: **Closure** is the tendency to perceive a complete familiar pattern even when part of it is missing. The broken circular shapes support the perception of a whole shape that is not fully drawn.
The **cloze procedure** applies completion to language. A reader uses the surrounding words to supply a missing word.
children: Successful completion depends on knowledge of the language. The answer must fit the pattern formed by the available words.

sections.title: What successful completion requires

teaching.text: **Completion** can test knowledge by asking a system to supply a missing part of a sequence. A successful answer shows that the system can use the pattern in the available information.
This approach treats an AI system’s knowledge in terms of its ability to complete sequences. **Prediction** is another way to describe supplying the expected continuation.

sections.title: From words to vectors and next-word probabilities

teaching.text: **GPT predicts the next word from the words supplied to it.** Each input word is represented by a **vector**, which is a list of numbers.
children: Different words receive different vectors. The numbers give the computer a representation it can use in calculations.

teaching.text: The output is a **probability distribution**. It assigns a probability to each possible next word.
children: For “chickens cackle and ducks,” **quack** should receive a high probability. An unrelated continuation such as “cat” should receive a low probability. The output represents several possibilities and how strongly each is predicted.

sections.title: Weights carry the system’s learned knowledge

teaching.text: **Weights** are numbers that hold the system’s learned knowledge. The input vectors represent the words supplied to the system, and the weights help transform those inputs into predictions.
The calculation uses operations such as addition, subtraction, multiplication and division. Its output is a **probability distribution** over possible next words.
children: The symbol **x** refers to an input, while **w** refers to a weight. They have different jobs even though both are numbers used in the calculation.

sections.title: Weights and synapses as a scale comparison

teaching.text: **Synapses** are connections between neurons in the brain. Knowledge of language involves an enormous network of these connections.
children: Knowing that chickens cackle and ducks quack depends on knowledge held in the brain’s connections. A large number of connections is therefore an important feature of the human system being studied.

teaching.text: The scale comparison concerns the **large number of connections or weights** in each system. A large number of weights in AI is not, by itself, a reason to dismiss a connection with human knowledge.

sections.title: Completion is a form of prediction

teaching.text: **Prediction** means using available information to anticipate a missing or upcoming part. In a sequence-completion task, predicting the continuation and completing the sequence describe the same task.
Treating knowledge as successful prediction is a proposal about what it means for an AI system to know something. It focuses attention on whether the system can produce an appropriate continuation.

sections.title: Mistakes provide a direction for learning

teaching.text: **Learning from mistakes** means using the difference between a prediction and the appropriate answer to improve the system. Making a prediction provides something that can be checked and corrected.
**Stochastic gradient descent, or SGD**, is a learning algorithm. A simple averaging problem makes its correction process easier to understand without requiring a complicated AI system.

sections.title: Averaging as observation-based error learning

teaching.text: **Observation-based error learning** starts with an estimate and improves it using individual observations. In the averaging example, the estimate is a guess about the average of a list of numbers.
children: Compare the estimate with one number from the list, then move the estimate partway toward that number. Repeating this with more observations allows the data to shape the estimate.

teaching.text: The important idea is **improvement through repeated corrections**. The estimate is learned from data instead of being obtained by directly adding the whole list and dividing.

sections.title: The correction rule of stochastic gradient descent

teaching.text: **Stochastic gradient descent** begins with an estimate, **x**, and compares it with a randomly selected observation, **d**. The difference between them is called the **loss** in this example.
children: Subtracting a small fraction of that difference moves the estimate toward the observation. If the estimate is above the observation, it moves down. If it is below the observation, it moves up.

teaching.text: The **learning rate** is the fraction used for each correction. A rate of 10% moves the estimate one tenth of the way toward the selected observation.

**Stochastic** refers to the random choice of observations. **Gradient** concerns the direction related to the loss, and **descent** concerns reducing the error. Repeated observations guide the estimate toward the average.

sections.title: Learning rate changes both speed and variability

teaching.text: The **initial condition**, or **IC**, is the starting estimate. The colored curves begin above, near and below the average, so they approach the same region from different directions.
The **learning rate** determines how much each observation changes the estimate.
children: A small rate produces smaller changes. The estimate approaches the average more slowly but fluctuates less.
A larger rate moves the estimate into the right region faster. Each new observation also pulls it farther, producing larger fluctuations around the average.

teaching.text: The starting estimate and the learning rate affect different aspects of learning. The starting estimate determines where the path begins, while the learning rate changes the size of its corrections.

sections.title: The speed–accuracy tradeoff

teaching.text: The **speed–accuracy tradeoff** concerns how quickly an estimate improves and how precisely it settles near the average.
children: A higher **learning rate**, written **γ**, gives observations more influence. The estimate changes quickly but continues to fluctuate more.
A lower learning rate makes each correction smaller. Learning is slower, but the estimate can remain closer to the average.

teaching.text: Improving an optimization method means trying to obtain both faster learning and greater accuracy. Changing the learning rate alone creates a tradeoff between those goals in these examples.

sections.title: Dynamical systems 1
Lecture agenda
Elements, relations, and a goal

teaching.text: A **dynamical system** can be understood through its **elements**, the **relations** between them and its **goal**. The elements are the parts, and the relations describe how those parts affect one another.
children: The goal identifies what the organized activity accomplishes. Describing the parts alone misses how their interactions produce the behavior of the whole system.

sections.title: An octopus coordinates its body with its environment

teaching.text: An octopus keeping its den uses its **eight arms**, the ground and its interactions with a fish as parts of an organized action. Its nervous system is distributed through its head and body.
The **relations** between the arms, ground and fish determine how the movements work together. Their shared **goal** is to keep the den.
children: Understanding the action requires explaining the coordination between parts, rather than treating each arm movement separately.

sections.title: Speech is an organized dynamical system

teaching.text: **Speech is a dynamical system** because several parts work together over time to convey a thought. Its elements include the tongue, lips, velum, larynx, palate and **pharyngeal wall**, the back wall of the throat.
children: The brain coordinates the relations between these parts. Producing speech depends on how their movements fit together, rather than on one structure acting alone.

sections.title: Shared organization across very different systems

teaching.text: **Dynamical systems** occur throughout the body. Voluntary actions and involuntary activity in the heart, pancreas and neurons all involve parts affecting one another over time.
The elements can be whole organs, parts of organs, cells or chemicals within cells. A system can therefore be studied at different physical scales.
children: Systems with very different elements can share patterns of organization. Recognizing those shared relations helps explain behavior across biology, chemistry and physics.

sections.title: Motor primitives combine into a complex octopus action

teaching.text: A complex octopus action can be analyzed into **motor primitives**, simpler movement components that combine to produce the full action. The slapping action involves coordinated changes in arm movement.
children: Components can combine in sequence and at the same time. Their organization helps explain how a flexible body produces a controlled action in relation to a moving fish.

teaching.text: The important question is how the movement components fit together to achieve the animal’s goal. A description of the separate parts alone does not explain the complete action.

sections.title: Knowledge and other psychological skills in AI

teaching.text: **AI models psychological abilities** including knowing, recognizing, attending, acting and learning. These abilities provide specific questions about what an artificial system can do.
In a **cloze task**, supplying a missing word tests knowledge through successful completion. This is one way to connect a psychological ability with an observable response.

sections.title: Inputs, knowledge, and a predicted distribution

teaching.text: A word enters GPT as a **vector**, a list of numbers used to represent it. The inputs are written **x**, and the word representations are called **tokens**.
The system combines the inputs with its **weights**, written **W**. These weights are numbers that hold learned knowledge and affect how the inputs are processed.
children: The calculations produce a **probability distribution** over possible next words. A high probability means the system strongly predicts that continuation.

sections.title: How initially random weights become useful

teaching.text: **Weights begin with random values.** These starting numbers allow the system to make a prediction, but they do not yet encode useful knowledge of the language.
A training sequence provides the answer against which to check the prediction. For “chickens cackle and ducks,” the target continuation is “quack.”
children: The weights are changed so the output assigns more appropriate probabilities. Repeating prediction and correction across many sequences builds the system’s learned knowledge.

sections.title: Random initialization and learning from mistakes

teaching.text: **Random initialization** gives the system its starting weights. **Learning from mistakes** changes those weights after its predictions are compared with appropriate answers.
children: Starting with random weights and improving them are different steps. Random values give learning a starting point, while corrections make the values useful for prediction.

sections.title: A simple model of learning an average

teaching.text: An average can be learned by **observation-based error learning**. Start with an estimate, compare it with one observation and move it partway toward that observation.
children: Each correction uses data to improve the estimate. The procedure repeats across observations instead of calculating the average directly from the full list.

sections.title: Start from an arbitrary estimate

teaching.text: The **estimate**, written **x**, is the current guess about the average. **x[0]** means the initial estimate, before any corrections.
children: The example starts at 130, above the data. This shows that the initial guess can be inaccurate and still provide a starting point for learning.

teaching.text: The **learning rate**, written **γ**, is 25%. Each update therefore moves the estimate one quarter of the way toward the selected observation.

sections.title: An observation exposes a discrepancy

teaching.text: The randomly selected observation is written **d**, and the current estimate is written **x**. Comparing them produces a **discrepancy**, called the **loss** in this example.
The estimate is 130 and the observation is 98. The estimate is too high relative to that observation, so the difference is positive.
children: The sign of this difference determines the direction of the correction. A positive difference calls for a decrease in the estimate.

sections.title: Correct a fraction rather than replacing the guess

teaching.text: With a **25% learning rate**, the estimate moves one quarter of the way toward the observation. The estimate is above the selected value, so subtracting part of the positive difference lowers it.
children: The red estimate moves downward toward the blue observation. It stops short of that observation because the correction uses only part of the difference.

sections.title: Correction after observation 2

teaching.text: The selected observation is **below the estimate**, so the correction lowers the estimate. The **learning rate** determines how much of the gap is removed.
children: The red line shows the estimate after each update. Its downward step means the guess has moved closer to the observation used for this correction.

sections.title: Correction after observation 3

teaching.text: An observation below the current guess produces a **positive discrepancy**. Subtracting a fraction of that discrepancy reduces the guess.
children: The estimate moves toward the selected observation, while the quarter-step correction leaves some distance between them. The rule changes the estimate without replacing it with the observation.

sections.title: Correction after observation 4

teaching.text: The selected value is lower than the estimate, so the **SGD correction moves downward**. The size of the change depends on both the gap and the learning rate.
children: A larger gap creates a larger correction at the same learning rate. The update brings the estimate closer to this observation.

sections.title: A high observation pulls the estimate upward

teaching.text: An observation **above the estimate** calls for an upward correction. The difference between the estimate and the observation is negative.
children: Subtracting part of a negative difference increases the estimate. The small rise in the red line shows that the same update rule can move the guess in either direction.

sections.title: Correction after observation 6

teaching.text: The selected observation lies **below the estimate**, so the difference is positive and the estimate moves down.
children: Each update responds to the observation selected for that step. The path can therefore change direction when observations fall on different sides of the current estimate.

sections.title: Correction after observation 7

teaching.text: The **current estimate exceeds the observation**. A correction removes one quarter of that difference, moving the estimate downward.
children: The red path records the updated estimates. Its movement reflects individual observations, while the green line marks the average of the complete data set.

sections.title: Correction after observation 8

teaching.text: A lower observation produces a **downward update**. The estimate is adjusted toward that particular observation rather than moved directly to the full-data average.
children: Different randomly selected observations produce different corrections. Their combined influence guides the estimate toward the region of the average.

sections.title: A high observation pulls the estimate upward

teaching.text: A higher observation produces a **negative discrepancy**, because the estimate minus the observation is negative. Subtracting a fraction of it raises the estimate.
children: The rise in the red path is an appropriate correction toward the selected datum. Learning does not require every update to point downward.

sections.title: Correction after observation 10

teaching.text: The observation is **close to the current estimate**, so their discrepancy is small. Using one quarter of a small discrepancy produces a small correction.
children: The short downward step reflects the size of this gap. The learning rate is unchanged.

sections.title: Correction after observation 11

teaching.text: The observation is below the current guess, and **SGD lowers the estimate**. The correction moves partway toward the observation.
children: The path fluctuates because the selected observations vary. A rise or fall in one update describes that observation’s effect, rather than a change in the learning rule.

sections.title: Correction after observation 12

teaching.text: The selected observation is lower than the estimate, so the **update moves downward**. The red estimate reaches the region of the green average line.
children: The algorithm has used individual observations and partial corrections. It has not obtained the average by adding the full list and dividing.

sections.title: Why the learning path jitters

teaching.text: **Stochastic gradient descent** improves an initial estimate through repeated corrections based on randomly selected observations.
children: **Stochastic** means the observation is selected at random. **Gradient** concerns the direction of correction related to the loss. **Descent** refers to reducing the mistake.

teaching.text: The path **jitters**, meaning it makes small changes in both directions. Different observations pull the estimate toward different values, while its overall tendency is toward the average.

sections.title: An estimate can fall while its loss falls

teaching.text: The estimate starts **above the average** and moves downward toward it. The upper graph shows the changing estimate, while the lower graph shows the **loss**.
In the lower graph, loss measures squared distance from the average. Getting closer makes this loss smaller.
children: Both curves fall in this example, but they represent different things. One is the value of the estimate, and the other is how far that estimate is from the target.

sections.title: An estimate can rise while its loss falls

teaching.text: The estimate starts **below the average**, so improvement requires it to rise. Its distance from the average shrinks as it approaches the target.
children: The **loss** still falls because it measures the squared distance. A rising estimate can therefore accompany a decreasing loss.

teaching.text: The direction of the estimate’s movement depends on its starting point. Learning concerns reducing the error, rather than always increasing or always decreasing the estimate.

sections.title: Learning rate and starting condition

teaching.text: The **initial condition**, or **IC**, is the starting estimate. The colored curves begin at different values but are pulled toward the same average.
The **learning rate** controls the fraction of each discrepancy used in an update.
children: Smaller learning rates make the curves approach slowly, with less variation near the average.
Larger rates bring the estimate into the correct region quickly, but produce wider fluctuations as individual observations pull it in different directions.

sections.title: The learning tradeoff

teaching.text: The **learning tradeoff** is between speed and accuracy. A larger **learning rate γ** produces bigger corrections, so learning is faster but the estimate fluctuates more around the average.
children: A smaller learning rate produces smaller corrections. Reaching the average takes longer, but the estimate stays closer to it.

teaching.text: Developing better **optimization** methods means trying to improve both speed and accuracy. Simply increasing or decreasing the rate has opposing effects on those two goals in this example.

lecture04.title: 04 · Dynamic programming and shared physical principles

sections.title: Dynamical systems 1
Lecture agenda
A staged shortest-path problem

teaching.text: The **shortest path problem** asks which route has the lowest total cost. A route begins at **A**, passes through states at successive stages and ends at **J**.
children: Each arrow has a cost. A route’s total cost is the sum of the costs of all its arrows.

teaching.text: The best route depends on the **whole path**. Selecting one inexpensive arrow does not establish that the complete route will have the lowest cost.

sections.title: Why the locally cheapest choice can lose

teaching.text: A **greedy algorithm** selects the lowest-cost arrow available at the current state. It repeats that local choice at each stage.
children: A cheap immediate step can lead to an expensive continuation. The algorithm can therefore produce a route whose total cost is higher than another available route.

teaching.text: The important difference is between the **cost of the next step** and the **total cost of reaching the destination**. Greedy choice based only on the next arrow ignores that distinction.

sections.title: Blank source page
Exhaustive search trades speed for certainty

teaching.text: An **exhaustive algorithm** checks every possible route and compares their total costs. Checking all possibilities allows it to identify the lowest-cost complete route.
children: The number of routes grows as more stages and states are added. Exhaustive search can therefore take a very long time, even though it finds the correct answer.

sections.title: Bellman’s decomposition

teaching.text: In **dynamic programming**, a state’s **value** is the best total cost of getting from that state to the destination. **V_BJ** means the best cost from B to J, and **V_CJ** means the best cost from C to J.
To find the best cost from A, compare the complete alternatives.
children: For the route through B, add the cost from A to B to the value of B. For the route through C, add the cost from A to C to the value of C.
The smaller total gives the **value of A**. Each comparison includes both the immediate step and the best remaining route.

sections.title: Solve the smaller problems that supply the values

teaching.text: The values of B and C are **subproblems** within the problem of finding the value of A. They must be solved before their answers can be used.
children: This is **Bellman’s decomposition**. Break the full problem into smaller problems whose solutions provide the information required by the larger problem.

sections.title: Propagating known costs backward

teaching.text: The value of B depends on the best costs from **D, E and F** to J. Each possible next step contributes its immediate cost plus the value of the state reached.
At the final stage, **G, H and I** connect directly to J. Their values can be read from those final arrows.
children: Those known values allow the values at the preceding stage to be calculated. Repeating this backward through the network supplies the values required at the start.

sections.title: Choose the best total after calculating values

teaching.text: **Calculate the values before choosing the route.** A value includes the best remaining cost, so it contains information missing from the cost of a single arrow.
Starting at A, compare the cost of each possible step **plus the value of the state it reaches**. Choose the alternative with the smallest combined cost.
children: Repeat this at each state until reaching J. The choices are local, but the calculated values make them account for the full remaining route.

sections.title: A value summarizes the relevant future

teaching.text: A **state value** summarizes the best total cost from that state to the destination. A costly obstacle near the end of a route therefore affects values calculated at earlier states.
children: This prevents an inexpensive initial arrow from appearing attractive when its continuation is expensive.

teaching.text: The values are calculated **backward** from the destination. The route is then followed **forward** from the start, using the stored values to select each step.

sections.title: Recursive breakdown and reconstruction

teaching.text: **Dynamic programming decomposes a problem into smaller subproblems.** If a subproblem still depends on unknown information, it is broken into smaller problems in turn.
children: The process reaches cases simple enough to solve directly. Their answers are then used to solve the larger problems that depend on them.

teaching.text: The full solution is built from these smaller solutions. A solved subproblem supplies an answer that can be reused wherever it is needed.

sections.title: The rule for propagating a value

teaching.text: **Bellman’s rule** calculates a state’s value by comparing its possible continuations. For each next state, add the immediate arrow cost to that next state’s value, then keep the smallest total.
Apply this rule from the last stage toward the first. Each state’s value becomes available when the values it depends on are known.
children: Reusing these values avoids recalculating the same remaining routes for every complete path. This is why **dynamic programming** can be much more efficient than exhaustive search.

sections.title: Least distance and least time can diverge

teaching.text: The **lowest total cost** can require choosing a more expensive initial step. That step can lead to a cheaper continuation and avoid a large cost near the end.

The **shortest distance** and **least time** are also different goals. When movement has the same speed everywhere, a straight route is fastest. When running on sand is faster than swimming, spending more of the route on sand can reduce the total time.
children: The best route depends on what is being minimized and on the costs of all its parts.

sections.title: Refraction shares the least-time principle

teaching.text: **Refraction** is the bending of light as it passes between media in which its speed differs. The route taken is a **least-time path**.
children: The fastest complete route can include different distances in the two media. Minimizing travel time is therefore different from requiring the shortest straight-line distance.

teaching.text: An optimization problem must account for the **total cost across the route**. In the network, a more expensive early arrow can be worthwhile if it avoids a greater cost in the continuation.

sections.title: Reading the completed state values

teaching.text: The numbers written at the states are **values**, meaning the best costs from those states to J. They are different from the costs written on individual arrows.
To identify the best route from A, compare each arrow’s cost **plus the value at its destination**. Choose the smallest total and continue in the same way.
children: The stored values make the complete remaining cost available at every decision. This allows the route to avoid expensive continuations that a raw-arrow greedy choice would miss.

sections.title: Pop quiz heading
Learning and coffee share approach to equilibrium

teaching.text: Both graphs show an **approach to equilibrium**, a value toward which the system tends. Estimates that begin above or below the average move toward the same region.
children: For the temperature curves, hot coffee cools and iced coffee warms toward room temperature. The change is larger when the temperature difference is larger and smaller near room temperature.

teaching.text: The shared pattern is **rapid change far from equilibrium and slower change near it**. The quantities are different, but both graphs describe change toward a stable level.

sections.title: Dynamical Systems 3
Homework reminder
Position and velocity change each other

teaching.text: A **harmonic oscillator** has two quantities that change together. **Position, x,** tells where something is relative to its resting position. **Velocity, v,** tells how its position is changing.
children: A dot above a letter means its **rate of change**, or how much it increases or decreases as time passes.

teaching.text: Velocity determines how position changes, while position determines how velocity changes in the opposite direction.
children: Positive velocity makes position increase. Positive position makes velocity decrease. The two rules connect position and velocity in a continuing loop.

sections.title: Read the sign of the change

teaching.text: A **negative velocity** makes position decrease. This describes the direction of motion, regardless of which side of the resting position the object is on.
A **negative position** makes velocity increase because the rule for changing velocity reverses the sign of position.
children: Increasing velocity can mean becoming less negative before becoming positive. It does not always mean speeding up in the current direction.

sections.title: Two different sign relationships

teaching.text: The rule for **position** follows the sign of velocity. If velocity is positive, position rises. If velocity is negative, position falls.
The rule for **velocity** reverses the sign of position. If position is positive, velocity falls. If position is negative, velocity rises.
children: Position and its rate of change are different quantities. An object can be on the positive side while moving toward smaller positions.

sections.title: Follow the position–velocity cycle

teaching.text: Suppose **position is negative and velocity is zero**. Negative position makes velocity rise above zero, and that positive velocity moves the object toward the resting position.
children: The object still has positive velocity when it reaches the resting position, so it continues into positive positions.

teaching.text: Once position is positive, velocity begins to fall. It reaches zero and then becomes negative, turning the motion back toward the other side.
children: This continuing change between position and velocity produces an **oscillation**, or repeated back-and-forth motion.

teaching.text: The position and velocity curves do not reach their peaks together. **Velocity is zero at a turning point**, but it can be large when position passes through zero.

sections.title: A closed feedback loop

teaching.text: The arrows between **position, x, and velocity, v,** form a **feedback loop**. Position changes velocity, and velocity changes position.
children: The effect returns to the quantity that started it, so the interaction continues. This repeated interaction produces the back-and-forth change called **oscillation** or **vibration**.

sections.title: Homework reminder
Harmonic oscillators across systems

teaching.text: A **harmonic oscillator** describes a repeating pattern of change. The same basic idea is useful for studying vibrations in different physical systems.

sections.title: Compression and rarefaction of air

teaching.text: During **compression**, air particles move closer together and pressure becomes higher. During **rarefaction**, the particles move farther apart and pressure becomes lower.
children: The particles stay the same size. What changes is the space between them.

teaching.text: The air slice repeatedly contracts and expands. Its **equilibrium spacing** is the spacing between the compressed and expanded states.
children: The highlighted pair follows that changing distance. The particle motion represents changing spacing rather than particles appearing or disappearing.

sections.title: Connect air motion to a cosine

teaching.text: A **cosine** describes the repeating expansion and compression of the air slice. The moving point on the curve shows the air spacing at that moment.
children: A positive value means the particles are farther apart than at equilibrium. Zero means equilibrium spacing. A negative value means the particles are closer together.

teaching.text: One **cycle** runs from maximum expansion through compression and back to maximum expansion.
children: The curve shows how expansion changes over time. It does not mean that individual air particles travel along a wavy path.

sections.title: Vowels depend on tongue position

teaching.text: **Tongue height** describes how high or low the tongue is. **Tongue backness** describes how far toward the front or back its raised region lies.
children: The vowels in **dean** and **dune** are both high. Dean is front, while dune is back.
The vowels in **Dan** and **Don** are low in this comparison. Dan is front, Don is back, and **done** is central.

teaching.text: These different tongue positions change the shape of the **vocal tract**, the air space above the vocal folds. The air has less room in some places and more room in others.

sections.title: Vowels combine more than one vibration

teaching.text: A vowel can combine **more than one frequency**. Each component is a repeating vibration, and adding the components produces a more complex pattern.
children: The two models combine different pairs of frequencies. Even though both air slices begin expanded, their spacing changes differently during the cycle.

teaching.text: The moving point follows the **combined vibration**. Positive values show rarefaction, and negative values show compression.
children: The deliberately slow frequencies make the motion visible. They illustrate how combining frequencies changes a pattern rather than giving measured frequencies of human vowels.

sections.title: Praat demonstration
Two vibrating parts of speech

teaching.text: Speech involves two physically different kinds of vibration. The **vocal folds** are tissue that opens and closes. The **air in the vocal tract** vibrates through changing compression and rarefaction.
children: The vocal folds provide the sound source that sets the air into vibration. Explaining the moving folds and explaining the moving air are separate parts of understanding speech.

sections.title: Economic cycles around a growth trend

teaching.text: The **business cycle** is a repeating rise and fall in economic output. Output rises during recovery, reaches a **peak**, falls during recession, and reaches a **trough** before rising again.
children: Time runs horizontally, while the level of output runs vertically.

teaching.text: The long-term **growth trend** rises even while the cycle moves above and below it. Repeated fluctuation can therefore occur around a baseline that is itself changing.

sections.title: Meadows reading reminder
Music and vibration

teaching.text: **Musical sound depends on vibration.** A repeating physical motion produces the changing sound pressure that makes a musical tone.

sections.title: Atoms, shell pictures and wave modes

teaching.text: Descriptions of atoms use **wave modes**, which are allowed patterns associated with electrons. A quantum **orbital** describes electron density rather than a tiny particle following a fixed circular path.
children: The magnesium comparison places a shell picture beside electron-density patterns. Darker regions represent greater density.

teaching.text: The total electron-density picture combines contributions from occupied orbitals. Those wave patterns differ from the historical drawing of electrons on paths.
children: Using wave modes in an atomic description does not make magnesium a simple classical harmonic oscillator.

sections.title: Python position–velocity demonstration
Dynamical Systems 5
Two quantities in an oscillator

teaching.text: **Position, x,** tells where something is relative to its resting position. **Velocity, v,** tells how position changes. A dot over a letter means its rate of change with time.
Velocity changes position, and position changes velocity with the sign reversed.
children: Positive velocity makes position rise. Positive position makes velocity fall.
Negative velocity makes position fall. Negative position makes velocity rise. These linked changes allow the motion to turn around repeatedly.

sections.title: Repeated change in a loop

teaching.text: **Oscillation**, or **vibration**, is repeated back-and-forth change. The arrows from position to velocity and back to position make a closed **feedback loop**.
children: A change in either quantity affects the other, which returns to affect the first. The repetition comes from this continuing interaction.

sections.title: Why a spring and a mass make vibration

teaching.text: A **spring** pulls a displaced system toward its resting position. **Stiffness** tells how strongly the spring pushes back for a given displacement.
**Mass** supplies the tendency to continue moving. The spring can bring a moving mass toward the resting position, but reaching that position does not automatically stop it.
children: The mass passes through the resting position. The spring then acts from the other side and turns it back. **Spring action and continued motion together produce vibration.**

teaching.text: Both **vocal-fold tissue** and **air in the vocal tract** vibrate during speech. Understanding the returning action and the moving material helps explain those vibrations.

sections.title: Air particles move closer and farther apart

teaching.text: **Compression** brings air particles closer together and raises pressure. **Rarefaction** spreads the particles farther apart and lowers pressure.
children: The same particles remain present and keep the same size. Their spacing changes as the air slice contracts and expands.

teaching.text: The dashed boundary marks **equilibrium spacing**. The highlighted pair moves closer together during compression and farther apart during rarefaction.
children: Air has the returning action needed for vibration because compressed air pushes back. It also has mass, so moving air can continue moving.

sections.title: Balancing feedback reduces displacement

teaching.text: **Negative feedback**, also called **balancing feedback**, reduces a difference from equilibrium. A positive displacement produces a change toward smaller values. A negative displacement produces a change toward larger values.
children: Both directions bring the system toward the same **equilibrium**, its resting position at zero.

teaching.text: The return is faster when the displacement is large. As the system approaches equilibrium, the displacement becomes smaller and so does the change it produces.
children: The curve therefore falls steeply at first and then flattens. Increasing the strength of the returning effect makes the approach faster.

sections.title: Mass carries motion onward

teaching.text: **Inertia** is the tendency of a mass to continue its motion unless something changes that motion. With **constant velocity**, it travels the same distance during each equal interval.
children: A moving mass does not stop simply because it reaches a particular place. This is why a mass moving toward equilibrium can pass through it.

sections.title: Returning to a place versus passing through it

teaching.text: **Displacement, x,** measures distance from the spring’s natural position. At **equilibrium**, x is zero.
children: In the spring-only model, a stretched spring approaches zero from one side. A compressed spring approaches it from the other side. Both settle toward the same position.

teaching.text: Attaching a **mass** changes the motion. The spring brings the mass toward equilibrium, but the mass is still moving when it arrives and carries on past it.
children: The spring now acts from the opposite side, slowing the mass and turning it back. Passing through equilibrium and turning around produce the repeated motion of an **oscillation**.

teaching.text: The oscillating trace crosses zero repeatedly, while its peaks become smaller. The resting position stays fixed even though the motion around it changes.

sections.title: Air expansion follows a cosine

teaching.text: The **cosine** curve follows the air slice as it expands and contracts. High points mean the particles are farthest apart, and low points mean they are closest together.
children: Positive values represent **rarefaction**. Negative values represent **compression**. Zero marks equilibrium spacing.

teaching.text: The curve describes the changing spacing over time. The air particles do not travel along the shape of the curve.
children: A complete **cycle** returns to the same spacing and stage of motion, such as from maximum rarefaction through compression and back to maximum rarefaction.

sections.title: Compare tongue configurations for vowels

teaching.text: **Vowel height** describes how high the tongue is, while **backness** describes how far forward or back its raised region lies.
children: The vowels in dean and dune are both high. Dean is front, and dune is back.
Dan is low and front, Don is low and back in this comparison, and done is central.

teaching.text: Moving the tongue changes where the **vocal tract** is narrow or wide. Changing that air space changes the way the air can vibrate.

sections.title: Frequency counts cycles in a fixed interval

teaching.text: **Frequency** tells how many complete cycles occur in a given time. Each air slice goes through compression and rarefaction, but the three slices complete different numbers of cycles.
children: The low-frequency example completes fewer cycles in the shared interval. The middle example completes twice as many, and the high example completes three times as many.

teaching.text: All three examples use the same range of particle spacing. **The amount of expansion and the frequency are different properties.** Air can expand by the same amount while repeating the motion faster or slower.

sections.title: Different combinations give different vowel patterns

teaching.text: A vowel pattern can combine **several vibrations at different frequencies**. The combined pattern depends on which frequencies are present.
children: The two models begin at the same expanded state but change differently during the interval. Their component vibrations do not stay lined up in the same way.

teaching.text: The graph follows the **combined air motion**. Positive values mean the particles are farther apart than at equilibrium, and negative values mean they are closer together.
children: These slow, illustrative models make the different patterns visible. They are not recordings of human vowels at those frequencies.

sections.title: Predict the effect of mass and stiffness

teaching.text: **Perturbation theory** predicts how a system changes when one of its properties changes. In a mass–spring system, **m** means mass, **k** means stiffness, and **f** means frequency.
children: Increasing mass lowers frequency when stiffness stays the same. A heavier mass is harder to slow and turn around, so each cycle takes longer.
Increasing stiffness raises frequency when mass stays the same. A stronger returning force turns the mass around sooner, so the cycle repeats faster.

sections.title: Hearing separates a mixture into frequencies

teaching.text: The **basilar membrane** inside the ear has different mass and stiffness along its length. Its heavier, less stiff end responds to lower frequencies, while its lighter, stiffer end responds to higher frequencies.
children: These responses follow the mass–stiffness relationship. Greater mass favors slower vibration, while greater stiffness favors faster vibration.

teaching.text: Neurons carry signals from different places along the membrane to the brain. **Where the vibration occurs** therefore provides information about which frequencies are present in the sound.

sections.title: Learning rate trades speed for steadiness

teaching.text: The **learning rate**, written gamma, controls how much an estimate changes after each observation. A high learning rate moves the estimate quickly, but it can keep bouncing around the answer.
children: A lower learning rate makes smaller changes. Learning is slower, but the estimate settles more steadily.

teaching.text: This is the **speed–accuracy tradeoff**. Fast movement toward an answer and a steady estimate are different goals, so changing the learning rate can improve one while making the other harder.

sections.title: Dynamical Systems 6
Exam reminder
A spring alone and a mass–spring system

teaching.text: The spring’s **equilibrium** is its natural resting position. In the spring-only model, displacement shrinks as the spring approaches that position.
children: A stretched spring returns from one side, while a compressed spring returns from the other.

teaching.text: A **mass–spring system** also has inertia. The spring moves the mass toward equilibrium, and the mass continues through it because it is already moving.
children: The spring then acts from the other side and turns the mass back. This interaction gives repeated crossings and turns, which make an **oscillation**.

sections.title: Mass, stiffness and the frequencies of speech

teaching.text: **Perturbation theory** predicts the effect of changing mass or stiffness. Increasing **mass, m,** lowers **frequency, f,** while increasing **stiffness, k,** raises frequency when the other property stays fixed.
children: More mass takes longer to turn around. A stiffer spring provides a stronger returning action.

teaching.text: During speech, changing the shape of the **vocal tract** changes how different portions of air behave. The air can vibrate at several frequencies, and the pattern differs between speech sounds.
children: The listener’s ear must separate the frequencies present in that pattern so that different speech sounds can be distinguished.

sections.title: The cochlea connects incoming sound to neural signals

teaching.text: The **cochlea** is the coiled part of the inner ear that sends the brain information about sound frequencies.
children: Sound vibrations enter through the outer ear and travel inward to the cochlea. The important connection is between incoming vibration and the neural signals used for hearing.

sections.title: The path into the basilar membrane

teaching.text: The **basilar membrane** runs along the inside of the cochlea. The membrane is coiled with it, but it can be understood as a long strip.
children: Sound vibration passes inward from the eardrum and the small connecting bones to the cochlea.

teaching.text: The membrane’s physical properties change along its length. Different parts can therefore respond most strongly to different frequencies rather than responding in exactly the same way.

sections.title: Frequency is represented by place and nerve activity

teaching.text: Different locations on the **basilar membrane** respond to different frequencies. The heavier, less stiff end responds to low frequencies. The lighter, stiffer end responds to high frequencies.
children: Greater mass favors slower motion, while greater stiffness favors faster motion.

teaching.text: The membrane is connected to **neurons** that carry signals to the brain. Activity at different locations tells the brain which frequencies are present in the incoming sound.

sections.title: How vocal folds make and change pitch

teaching.text: The **vocal folds** are small muscles with both mass and stiffness. Other muscles can stretch them to make them stiffer or bunch them to make them effectively heavier.
children: Stiffer folds vibrate faster. Heavier folds vibrate more slowly. Their vibration rate is the **fundamental frequency, F0**, which is closely connected with pitch.

teaching.text: Changing this vibration rate allows singing and conveys information in speech. In English, pitch changes can signal questions, surprise or emotion. In a **tone language**, pitch differences can distinguish word meanings.
Vibration begins when air pressure builds beneath closed folds and pushes them apart. Air flows through the opening, and the airflow draws the folds inward again.
children: The source calls this inward effect the **Bernoulli force**. Pressure can then push the folds apart again, repeating the opening-and-closing cycle.

sections.title: Position-first updates keep the oscillator bounded

teaching.text: The oscillator uses **position, x,** and **velocity, v,** to compute a sequence of states. At each step, velocity is used to update position, and the **new position** is then used to update velocity.
children: The update takes a small step through time rather than trying to compute the entire motion at once.

teaching.text: The position curve moves through high and low values, while velocity reaches zero at the turning points. Position passes through zero while velocity is still nonzero.
children: In this position-first procedure, the plotted swings stay near their original range. The order of the updates is part of the algorithm, not an interchangeable detail.

sections.title: Explicit Euler uses the old pair for both updates

teaching.text: **Explicit Euler** updates both position and velocity from the **previous pair of values**. The velocity update therefore uses the old position, even if a new position has already been calculated.
With the displayed time step, the computed swings grow larger across cycles. That growth comes from the numerical approximation rather than from an extra physical force in the oscillator.
children: The same intended system can produce a different numerical result when an update uses a different version of the state. The time step and update rule affect how well the simulation follows the intended motion.

sections.title: Arithmetic can approximate continuous change

teaching.text: **Euler’s explicit method** turns a rule about change into repeated arithmetic. It takes the previous value and adds the estimated change over a small time step.
children: Repeating this operation builds an approximate sequence of states. A computer can therefore follow a system’s changing behavior using a simple operation again and again.

teaching.text: The result is an **approximation**. Its accuracy depends on the time step and the way the update is performed.

Differential equations express how systems change

teaching.text: A **differential equation** describes a relationship involving a rate of change. It connects what a system is doing now with how its quantities change over time.
children: This is the mathematical form of a **dynamical system**, a system whose state develops through time.

teaching.text: Knowing a rule for change helps predict a system’s behavior from a starting state. The same broad perspective connects physical systems with learning and inference in language models.

sections.title: Predict a return toward equilibrium step by step

teaching.text: **Negative feedback**, or **balancing feedback**, makes the change oppose the current displacement. A value above zero decreases toward zero, while a value below zero increases toward zero.
children: The farther the system is from **equilibrium**, the larger its return-driving change. As the displacement shrinks, the return slows.

teaching.text: **Euler’s method** uses the current value to estimate the next value. Applying the same rule repeatedly gives a sequence that approaches equilibrium.
children: The curve is steep at first and then flattens because the remaining difference becomes smaller. The repeated arithmetic approximates this changing process.
