Software 1.0
A signal becomes a distribution over identities

teaching.text: A **neural network** takes an input represented by numbers and produces an output about its identity. Image pixels can be used to identify a face, and speech-wave values can be used to identify a speech sound.
The output is a **probability distribution**, with one probability for each possible answer. Those probabilities add up to **one**, or 100%.
children: For the five vowels ordered read, rad, rude, Rud and rod, the example assigns its largest probability to the third category. That makes **rude** the best-supported answer.
The agreed category order matters because each position in the list has a specific meaning.

sections.title: Learning changes the weights after an error

teaching.text: The input is a **vector**, a list of numbers representing the signal. The network combines that input with its **weights**, the numbers that hold its learned knowledge.
children: The input values can be positive or negative. They are signal measurements, not output probabilities.

teaching.text: **Forward propagation** computes an answer using the current weights. With initially random weights, the answer can be wrong.
children: For the vowel in Rud, the correct target puts a one in Rud’s position and zeros in the other positions. Comparing the computed answer with that target gives an **error**, or **loss**.

teaching.text: **Learning** changes the weights to reduce the loss. The process repeats with other signals whose correct identities are known.
children: The network improves its knowledge by changing weights, rather than by changing which signal was presented.

sections.title: Template matching and successive representations

teaching.text: A recognizer receiving the speech sound **[z]** should identify it as [z], rather than [s] or [a]. Two ideas help explain how a neural network can turn a signal into that decision.
**Templatic perception** compares incoming information with stored patterns. **Hierarchical perception** processes information through several stages.
children: A network can combine the two by comparing numerical patterns at successive stages before making its output decision.

sections.title: Templates make familiarity into a comparison

teaching.text: In **templatic perception**, an incoming pattern is compared with stored **templates**, the internal patterns for familiar objects.
children: For face recognition, the incoming face is compared with familiar-face templates. The closest match determines the perceived identity and, when available, the associated name.

teaching.text: A neural network’s **weights** provide numerical patterns for comparison. Learning makes those patterns more useful for identifying the input.
children: Before learning, poor weights can give a poor match and an incorrect decision.

sections.title: Perception involves connected stages

teaching.text: **Hierarchical perception** builds a decision through several stages. A **representation** is the form in which a stage holds or describes the information.
children: One stage transforms the input into a new representation. That result becomes information that another stage can transform again.

teaching.text: The connected brain areas show that perception involves interaction between stages. The arrows include several routes and returning connections, rather than a single isolated step from input to decision.

sections.title: An inner product compares two numerical patterns

teaching.text: An **inner product** compares an input vector with a template vector. Each input value is multiplied by the template value in the matching position, and the products are added.
children: The lists must have the same number of entries so their positions can be paired.

teaching.text: In the example, the second template produces the stronger positive result and is the better match under this comparison rule.
children: A large positive inner product indicates a stronger match, while a result near zero indicates little match. The result is a comparison score, not an output probability.

sections.title: Inference uses weights and learning improves them

teaching.text: **Inference** uses the current weights to compute an answer for an input signal. Inner products compare numerical patterns, and several stages turn those comparisons into an output.
**Learning** uses an input with a known identity to improve the weights. The network first performs inference, compares its answer with the target, and then changes the weights to reduce the error.
children: **Stochastic gradient descent, SGD,** supplies the weight updates. Computing an answer and improving the weights are different operations, even though a learning step includes both.

sections.title: Neural Networks 1.5
Exam and pencil reminder
The input signal and the output decision

teaching.text: A **neural network** receives numbers representing a signal and returns a **probability distribution** over possible identities.
children: For a face, the input contains pixel values. For speech, the input can contain pressure values from the waveform. The input measurements are different from the possible output categories.

teaching.text: Each output position belongs to one category, and the probabilities add up to **one**, or 100%.
children: With vowels ordered read, rad, rude, Rud and rod, the largest probability in the example belongs to **rude**, the third vowel. The list means something only when its category order is known.

sections.title: Learned weights support recognition

teaching.text: A network’s **weights** are the numbers that carry its learned knowledge. The network combines an input **vector**, a list of signal values, with those weights to compute an output.
**Forward propagation** is the computation from input to output using the current weights. Random starting weights can give the wrong answer.
children: For an input whose correct identity is Rud, the target puts a one at Rud’s position and zeros elsewhere. The difference between this target and the computed output gives the **loss**, or error.

teaching.text: During **learning**, the weights change to reduce that error. Repeating prediction, comparison and adjustment with many known examples improves the network’s decisions.

sections.title: Inference is part of learning

teaching.text: **Inference** combines the input with the current weights to compute an output. **Learning** determines how those weights should change.
children: A learning step must compute the current answer before comparing it with the correct answer. Inference is therefore part of learning, but computing an output by itself does not improve the weights.

sections.title: A receiving neuron combines weighted inputs

teaching.text: An **activation** is the numerical signal associated with a unit. A **weight** controls how an incoming activation contributes to the receiving unit.
children: Each connection has its own weight. The receiving unit multiplies each incoming activation by its weight and adds the results.

teaching.text: This **weighted sum** is also called an **inner product**, **scalar product**, or **dot product**.
children: The sign of the contribution depends on both the input and the weight. A negative input multiplied by a negative weight gives a positive contribution, while a positive input multiplied by a negative weight gives a negative contribution.

teaching.text: The retinal drawing shows connected biological neurons. The signed numbers form an arithmetic model of selected connections rather than a claim that biological neurons literally contain those numbers.

sections.title: From neural activity to arithmetic models

teaching.text: Mathematical **neural-network models** express selected ideas about neurons as numerical operations. The historical examples show continuing attempts to describe neural processing using arithmetic.
children: The connection is a modelling idea. An arithmetic operation can represent an aspect of neural activity even though numbers and biological tissue are physically different.

sections.title: Two views of the relationship between AI and brains

teaching.text: One view treats modern AI and human thinking as fundamentally different because numerical calculations differ from brain chemistry and electrical activity. Another view treats AI as a history of attempts to model aspects of brain activity with arithmetic.
children: These are competing **beliefs about the models**, rather than a demonstrated count of how many people hold each view. This material is **outside the exam**.

sections.title: Forward propagation through a multilayer perceptron

teaching.text: A **multilayer perceptron** has an input layer, **hidden layers**, and an output layer. Hidden layers are the processing stages between the input and the final answer.
children: Every unit in one layer connects to every unit in the next. Each connection has a weight that affects the receiving unit’s calculation.

teaching.text: A hidden unit combines the previous layer’s activations through an **inner product**. Its result becomes a new activation.
children: The activations in one hidden layer become the inputs to the next. **Forward propagation** repeats this process from the input toward the output.

teaching.text: The output uses **softmax** to turn the final values into probabilities that add up to one. The category with the largest probability is the best-supported decision.
children: Hidden activations can be negative in this example. Output probabilities cannot, because they describe how the network distributes its answer among the categories.

sections.title: A changed input and changed weights change the activation

teaching.text: The requested **activation** belongs to the second neuron in Hidden 1. To obtain it, pair each input value with the weight on its connection to that neuron.
children: Multiply each pair and add the contributions. The result is the neuron’s **inner product**.

teaching.text: Both the inputs and the weights matter. A changed input or a changed weight can change the contribution, its sign, and the final activation.
children: The displayed answer is negative because the negative contributions outweigh the positive ones. This is still the same weighted-sum operation.

sections.title: Exam and pencil reminder
Use an output error to improve the weights

teaching.text: **Training** begins with an input whose correct output is known. The **target** identifies the correct category by putting a one in its position and zeros in the other positions.
children: Here the target identifies the sixth category. The computed output favors the fourth category instead, so the current answer disagrees with the target.

teaching.text: The disagreement gives an **error**, or **loss**. **Backpropagation** works backward through the layers to determine how the weights contributed to that error.
children: **Stochastic gradient descent, SGD,** uses this information to adjust the weights in a direction that reduces the loss.

teaching.text: Prediction, comparison and adjustment repeat across many input–output pairs. **Inference** uses the current weights, while **learning** changes them.

sections.title: An erroneous observation changes what gets learned

teaching.text: The average-estimation data contain a mistake. Most observations are much lower than **400**, the value identified as erroneous.
children: Including that mistake pulls the average to about **100**. Without it, the average is about **80**. The numbers show how one bad observation can distort the quantity being learned.

teaching.text: An update based on the mistaken value pulls the estimate toward it. **Learning from supplied data does not automatically correct errors in those data.**
children: A small update limits how much a single observation changes the estimate, but it does not establish that the observation is valid.

lecture11.title: Masses and Springs · Theory and Prediction

sections.title: Masses and Springs · Theory and Prediction
One mass, two directions

teaching.text: A spring pulls a displaced mass toward **equilibrium**, its resting position. The mass has **inertia**, meaning that its motion continues instead of stopping as soon as it reaches that position.
children: If the spring is stretched and the mass is released, the spring pulls the mass back. The mass then passes equilibrium, compresses the spring and is pushed back in the other direction. This repeated motion is **vibration**.

teaching.text: Returning to equilibrium is different from stopping there. At equilibrium the spring has reached its resting length, but **the mass can still be moving**.
The same vibration can be shown as **longitudinal motion**, left and right along the spring, or **transverse motion**, up and down between the supports.
children: In the transverse drawing, pulling the mass upward stretches the springs. They pull it down toward the middle, and the moving mass continues through the middle. The direction changes, but the explanation of the cycle stays the same.

sections.title: Mass and stiffness change the rate

teaching.text: The number of complete cycles in a second is the **frequency**. This describes **how quickly the motion repeats**, rather than how far the mass moves.
With the spring unchanged, **a heavier mass lowers frequency**. More mass is harder to turn around, so the return trip takes longer.
With the mass unchanged, **a stiffer spring raises frequency**. The stronger restoring pull turns the mass around sooner.
children: Each row changes one property while holding the other fixed. The comparison therefore separates the effect of mass from the effect of stiffness.
Both directions of motion show the same result. Mass and stiffness determine the rate, rather than the orientation of the drawing.

sections.title: Two masses have two normal modes

teaching.text: **Mode 1 and mode 2 are patterns of the whole system, not names for the two masses.** Both masses take part in each pattern.
In **mode 1**, the masses move together, both up and both down, or both left and both right.
children: Their separation stays the same, so the middle spring does not stretch or compress. Only the outer springs provide the changing pull.

teaching.text: In **mode 2**, the masses move against each other. One moves up while the other moves down, or one moves left while the other moves right.
children: Their changing separation stretches and compresses the middle spring. All three springs now contribute to the restoring action. This greater use of stiffness makes **mode 2 faster than mode 1**, even though the masses and springs are unchanged.

teaching.text: The bottom row combines **both modes**. Starting both masses above equilibrium, with one higher than the other, produces motion that is partly together and partly against each other.
children: This combined pattern does not add a third mode. It adds the motions of the two available modes.

sections.title: Pop quiz
Three masses have three normal modes

teaching.text: **Three masses allow three modes**, each with its own pattern and frequency.
In **mode 1**, all three masses move together. There is relatively little stretching between neighboring masses, so this is the lowest-frequency pattern.
In **mode 2**, the two outer masses move against each other while **the middle mass remains still**.
children: Leaving the middle mass undisturbed and moving the outer masses in opposite directions starts this pattern. A still middle mass remains part of the three-mass system.

teaching.text: In **mode 3**, the middle mass moves against the two outer masses. When the outer masses rise together, the middle mass falls.
children: Neighboring masses pull against each other more strongly than in the other patterns. There is more stretching and compression, so mode 3 has the highest frequency.

teaching.text: The bottom row is a **combination of the three modes**, not a fourth mode. Several patterns can contribute to the movement at the same time.

sections.title: One more mass, one more mode

teaching.text: For these chains, **N masses give N modes**. N means the number of masses. A two-mass chain has two modes, and a six-mass chain has six.
The lowest mode has the masses moving together. Higher modes divide the chain into more regions moving against one another.
children: In the second mode, the left and right parts move in opposite directions. With an odd number of masses, the middle mass stays still.
More motion against neighboring parts creates more stretching and compression, so the higher modes have higher frequencies.

teaching.text: A **string** has mass and springiness throughout its length. Treating it as many small connected masses and springs explains how it can support the same kinds of vibration patterns.
children: The modes of a chain with separate masses are not generally exact whole-number multiples of the lowest frequency.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics

teaching.text: Both ends of a **fixed–fixed string** stay still. The first mode has one moving section, the second has two opposing sections, and higher modes fit more sections into the same length.
The frequencies are **harmonics**, meaning whole-number multiples of the lowest or **base frequency**. The second is twice the first, the third is three times the first, and so on.
children: Frequency is measured in **Hertz**, or cycles per second.

teaching.text: The combined string adds the motions of its active modes. A complex-looking movement can therefore contain several simple vibration patterns.
In the **spectrum**, a spike’s position tells its **frequency**, and its height tells its **amplitude**, or strength.
children: A taller spike means more of that vibration is present. It does not mean the vibration is faster.
Five active modes produce five spikes. A single active mode produces one spike at its own frequency.

sections.title: A membrane combines spatial modes

teaching.text: A **membrane** is a surface that can vibrate. Its moving parts extend in two directions, so its modes divide the surface into regions rather than dividing only a line.
children: The first mode rises and falls as one region. Other modes have neighboring regions moving against one another, with still lines between them.

teaching.text: Several modes can occur together. Their motions add to make the changing surface shown in the combined panel.
children: The spectrum shows a spike for each active frequency. The equally spaced frequencies in this demonstration are assigned for illustration, rather than calculated as the natural frequencies of this rectangle.

teaching.text: The **vocal folds** are vibrating tissue with many moving parts. Describing their motion in modes connects that movement with the frequencies present in a voice.

sections.title: Theory makes a measurable prediction

teaching.text: A **theory** explains how a system behaves, while a **prediction** states what should appear in a measurement. **Differential equations** express the changes that the theory describes.

For the vocal folds, the prediction is **evenly spaced harmonics** in the spectrum of laryngeal vibration. The first peak gives the base frequency, and the other peaks occur at its whole-number multiples.
A recording tested in **Praat** shows regularly spaced peaks. The check concerns the **spacing between peaks**, rather than memorizing one person’s frequency.
children: A second voice can have a higher base frequency and wider harmonic spacing. Both voices support the prediction when each has peaks at multiples of its own base frequency.

sections.title: One fixed end and one free end

teaching.text: The fixed end of a **fixed–free system** cannot move. It is a **node**. The free end has the largest motion and is an **antinode**.
Every allowed mode must keep those endpoint conditions. Its frequencies follow **one, three, five, seven** times the lowest frequency.
children: **The second mode is the second allowed pattern**, so its frequency is three times the lowest frequency. “Second mode” does not mean twice the frequency.
Each higher pattern adds internal nodes and opposing moving regions while retaining motion at the free end.

teaching.text: With length and wave speed unchanged, the lowest frequency is **half** that of a string fixed at both ends.

lecture12.title: Masses and Springs in Speech Production

sections.title: Masses and Springs in Speech Production
Dynamic systems in economic stabilization

teaching.text: **Stabilization** concerns keeping a system near **equilibrium** and reducing large swings. **Balancing feedback** counters a departure from that balance.
The economic example tracks unemployment and inflation as they change over time. A policy that **damps** a fluctuation makes its swings smaller.
**DSGE** stands for **Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium**. Dynamic refers to change over time, and stochastic refers to unpredictable events that disturb the system.
children: The theory therefore includes both ongoing change and unexpected shocks, rather than assuming that nothing disturbs the balance.

sections.title: One mass, two directions

teaching.text: The spring pulls a displaced mass toward **equilibrium**, its resting position. The mass keeps moving as it reaches that position, passes it and is pushed back from the other side. The result is **vibration**.
In **longitudinal motion**, the mass moves left and right along the spring. In **transverse motion**, it moves up and down between the supports.
children: Both drawings show a restoring pull together with the mass’s continued motion. Changing the drawing’s direction does not change that explanation.

sections.title: Mass and stiffness change the rate

teaching.text: **Frequency** counts complete cycles per second. Adding mass lowers frequency when the spring stays the same, because a heavier mass is harder to turn around.
Adding **stiffness** raises frequency when the mass stays the same. The spring pulls back harder for the same displacement, so the return takes less time.
children: The longitudinal and transverse drawings show the same directions of change. More mass slows the repeating movement, and more stiffness speeds it up.

sections.title: Two masses have two normal modes

teaching.text: The two masses have **two modes**, or patterns of vibration. Both masses participate in either mode.
In **mode 1**, the masses move together. The middle spring moves with them without stretching or compressing, so the outer springs supply the restoring pull.
In **mode 2**, the masses move against each other. The middle spring stretches and compresses as well as the outer springs.
children: The extra contribution from the middle spring makes the system effectively stiffer in mode 2. **Mode 2 therefore has a higher frequency**, even though the same masses and springs are present in both modes.

teaching.text: Lifting both masses to different heights starts **both modes together**. The bottom row combines their motions rather than adding a new mode.

sections.title: Three masses have three normal modes

teaching.text: A three-mass system has **three modes**. Mode 1 moves all three masses together. Mode 2 moves the outer masses against each other while the middle stays still. Mode 3 moves the middle against both outer masses.
The effect of **stiffening a spring** depends on how much that spring stretches and compresses in a particular mode.
children: If a spring only moves along with its neighbors, increasing its stiffness contributes little. If its length changes strongly, more stiffness raises that mode’s frequency.

teaching.text: Increasing the **middle mass** slows modes 1 and 3, where that mass moves. It leaves mode 2 unchanged, where that mass stays still.
children: **The same physical change affects different modes differently.** The mass has not been moved to a new location. Its role changes because the pattern changes.
The middle mass moves more in mode 3 than in mode 1, so the frequency drop is greater in mode 3.

sections.title: One more mass, one more mode

teaching.text: **N masses give N modes** in these chains. The first mode moves the masses together. The second divides them into two opposing regions, and the third has the middle region moving against the sides.
children: Higher modes involve more stretching between neighboring parts and have higher frequencies.

teaching.text: A **string** has both mass and springiness along its length. A chain with more and more connected masses and springs approaches that continuous system.
A vibrating string can contain **several modes at once**. Adding those simple patterns produces the complicated movement of the whole string. A **pure tone** contains just one frequency.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics

teaching.text: The modes of an ideal **fixed–fixed string** have frequencies that are **harmonics**, whole-number multiples of the lowest or **base frequency**.
The first mode contains one moving section. The second fits two opposing sections into the same string length, and the third fits three.
children: Fitting more sections into the same length makes the waves shorter and the frequency higher. The second mode vibrates twice as fast as the first, and the third vibrates three times as fast.

teaching.text: The combined string adds the motions of several modes. Its **spectrum** separates that combined motion into frequencies.
children: A spike’s position gives its frequency, and its height gives its amplitude. The equal spike heights are a setting of this demonstration.

sections.title: Mass, stiffness, position, and frequency

teaching.text: The symbols **m** and **k** mean mass and stiffness. **More mass lowers frequency, while more stiffness raises it.** The downward arrow printed beside stiffness in the first line is a typo, corrected by the stiffness principle below it.

For added mass, ask whether the changed part **moves in that mode**. More movement means a greater frequency drop. At a node, where that part stays still throughout the cycle, added mass has no effect.
For added stiffness, follow the **stretching or compression between neighboring parts**. A still point can sit between parts that strongly stretch against one another.
children: A node is not simply a point caught at equilibrium for one instant. It remains still through the cycle. This is why a snapshot alone cannot identify every node.

teaching.text: A chain with **N masses has N modes**. Fixed–fixed string modes have whole-number harmonic frequencies, while fixed–free modes have odd-multiple frequencies.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics

teaching.text: In the first mode of this fixed–fixed string, the **middle moves most**, while the ends stay still. The middle region moves up and down with little stretching between nearby parts.
Near a fixed end there is little movement, but neighboring parts stretch against one another. **Strong motion and strong stretching occur in different regions.**
children: Higher modes repeat this alternation at more places along the string. A local change must therefore be matched to the pattern of the mode being examined.

sections.title: A local change affects two modes differently

teaching.text: Both changes are made at **the same marked location**. Mode 4 moves strongly there. Mode 5 has a still point there, with strong stretching around it.
For **mode 4**, adding mass slows the moving section and lowers frequency. Stiffening that section has little effect because it does little stretching.
For **mode 5**, adding mass to a point that stays still does not slow the mode. Increasing stiffness does matter because neighboring parts stretch against one another there, so frequency rises.
**Making one section heavier and stiffer lowers mode 4 and raises mode 5.** The opposite results come from how each mode uses the location.
children: This reasoning is **perturbation**, predicting what a small change does to the system. Adding mass to a moving region of a drum lowers a frequency, while adding it at a still point leaves that mode unchanged.

sections.title: A membrane combines spatial modes

teaching.text: A **membrane** is a vibrating surface. Its first mode moves as one region, while higher modes have more regions moving against one another.
children: The two-number labels identify how the surface is divided in its two directions. A pattern with two regions in one direction has those regions moving oppositely.

teaching.text: Several membrane modes can occur **at the same time**. Their motions add to make the combined surface, and the spectrum has a spike for each active frequency.
children: The equally spaced frequencies and equal spike heights are assigned for this illustration. They are not a calculation of this rectangle’s natural frequencies.

teaching.text: The **vocal folds** contain many connected moving parts, so their vibration can also be described through modes.

sections.title: Theory makes a measurable prediction

teaching.text: The predicted **harmonics** are evenly spaced peaks in the spectrum of vocal-fold vibration. A spectral slice in **Praat** tests whether the peaks occur at multiples of the base frequency.
The measured second and third peaks are about twice and three times the first. A different voice can have a different starting frequency and still show the same pattern.
Changing the **mass or stiffness of part of the vocal folds** can change how they vibrate. A nodule adds mass locally, and its effect depends on which parts move in the different modes.
children: This application concerns a change in the vibrating tissue, rather than a change in the air resonances used to shape vowels.

sections.title: One fixed end and one free end

teaching.text: **Fixed and free describe motion at the ends of the model.** A node stays still, while an antinode has maximum motion. Every fixed–free mode must retain a node at one end and an antinode at the other.
The allowed frequencies follow **one, three, five** times the lowest frequency. The second allowed mode therefore has three times the first mode’s frequency.
children: For the same length and wave speed, the lowest frequency is half that of a string fixed at both ends.

teaching.text: In the idealized **vocal tract**, the vocal-fold end is closed to the air’s back-and-forth motion, while the open lips permit that motion.
children: The air can vibrate in several modes at once. Its fixed–free endpoint conditions apply to every one of those modes.

sections.title: Air in a fixed–free tube has modes

teaching.text: The air in the **vocal tract** both moves and compresses. Its mass contributes **inertia**, while compression and expansion reveal its **springiness**.
children: The chain is fixed at the **glottis**, the opening between the vocal folds, and free at the lips. These labels describe whether air can move back and forth at each end.

teaching.text: A **formant** is a resonance of the air in the vocal tract, a frequency at which that air vibrates strongly. **F1** names the lowest resonance, and **F2** names the second.
children: In the uniform fixed–free tube, F2 is three times F1. The number 2 orders the formants. It does not mean twice F1.
The marks at one third and two thirds of the tract length are measured from the glottis. The free end is the lip location.

sections.title: Vowel shape locates a constriction

teaching.text: A **constriction** is a narrowing of the vocal tract. Vowels differ in where the tongue or lips create that narrowing.
children: **High** and **low** describe tongue height. **Front**, **central** and **back** describe its position from front to back.

teaching.text: The high front vowel in **Dean** has a constriction near two thirds of the distance from the glottis. **Dune** has rounding at the lips. **Don** has a constriction near one third of the distance from the glottis.
children: **Done** is the central example with no marked constriction. **Dan** is shown as low and front.

teaching.text: The constriction’s **location** matters because the air does different amounts of moving and compressing at different places in each mode.

sections.title: Blank source page
Air in a fixed–free tube has modes

teaching.text: The same location can behave differently in **mode 1 and mode 2**. Near the lips, both modes have strong motion. Farther inside the tract, one mode can have strong motion where another has strong compression.
**F1 and F2 are air resonances**, not the harmonics of the vocal folds. A constriction changes a formant according to what the air does at that location in its mode.
children: The /a/ mark is near one third of the distance from the glottis. The /i/ mark is near two thirds, and /u/ marks the lip end.

sections.title: /u/ loads the moving lip end

teaching.text: Lip rounding for **/u/** increases the effective mass of air near the lips. This is **loading the free end**.
Both mode 1 and mode 2 have **strong motion and little compression** there. The extra mass slows both modes, while the extra stiffness has little effect.
children: **F1 goes down and F2 goes down.** The location’s behavior explains why both formants move in the same direction.

sections.title: /i/ has opposite effects on F1 and F2

teaching.text: The constriction for **/i/** lies near two thirds of the distance from the glottis. Narrowing the tract there increases both effective mass and stiffness.
In **mode 1**, the air mostly moves back and forth. More moving mass slows the cycle, so **F1 goes down**.
In **mode 2**, the air mostly compresses and expands. More stiffness makes the restoring action stronger, so **F2 goes up**.
children: The two effects do not cancel because motion matters more in one mode and compression matters more in the other.

sections.title: /a/ reverses the two effects

teaching.text: The /a/ constriction is near **one third of the distance from the glottis**. It makes that part of the air heavier and stiffer.
Mode 1 has strong compression there, so the stiffness increase raises **F1**. Mode 2 has strong motion there, so the mass increase lowers **F2**.
children: **F1 goes up and F2 goes down.** The prediction follows the local motion and compression in each mode, rather than a rule that every constriction raises or lowers every formant.

sections.title: Mass, stiffness, position, and frequency

teaching.text: A local change affects a mode according to **what changes and what that location does**. Added mass lowers frequency when the part moves. Added stiffness raises frequency when neighboring parts stretch or compress.
The symbols **m** and **k** stand for mass and stiffness. Raising both at one location does not guarantee cancellation, because their influence depends on the mode.
children: At a still point, more mass has little effect but more stiffness can matter strongly. At a strongly moving location with little stretching, more mass matters most.

sections.title: Compression and motion alternate in an air column

teaching.text: Follow both **how far a line of air moves** and **how its distance from neighboring lines changes**. The first is motion, and the second reveals compression and expansion.
At the open lips, neighboring lines move back and forth together with little change in their spacing. This region has strong motion but little compression.
Near the closed end, the air cannot move far, but neighboring lines repeatedly crowd together and spread apart. This region has strong compression.
children: A line that stays still can have neighboring air moving toward and away from it. Stillness at a point therefore does not remove springiness around it.

teaching.text: The higher modes fit more alternating motion and compression regions into the same tract. The effect of a constriction must be checked separately for each formant.
