sections.title: Masses and Springs in Speech Production
Mass, stiffness, position, and frequency

teaching.text: Raising **mass** tends to lower frequency, and raising **stiffness** tends to raise it. Those opposite tendencies do not establish that the effects are equal.
Cancellation requires the effective changes to **balance**. In a system with many parts, the mode’s motion and stretching at the changed location determine how strongly each effect counts.

Where a point stays still but nearby parts stretch strongly, added mass has no effect while added stiffness raises frequency. Where motion is strong and stretching is weak, added mass lowers frequency while added stiffness contributes little.
children: The change can therefore raise one mode’s frequency and lower another’s even when the same part becomes both heavier and stiffer.

sections.title: One more mass, one more mode

teaching.text: These chains have equal masses and springs, with both ends fixed. **N masses give N modes**, so each row has as many possible patterns as it has masses.
The lowest mode moves the masses together. Higher modes divide the chain into more regions moving against one another.
children: More relative movement between neighbors means more stretching and compression, which makes the higher-frequency patterns faster.

teaching.text: A chain with separate masses does not generally have frequencies that are exact whole-number multiples. The **ideal string** is the continuous system with that harmonic relationship.

sections.title: Why fixed–fixed frequencies are integer multiples

teaching.text: A string fixed at both ends must have **no motion at each end**. The first mode contains one **half-wave packet**, a section that runs from a still point through a moving region to another still point.
The second mode fits two half-wave packets into the same length, and the fifth fits five. More packets mean shorter waves and higher frequencies.
children: The second harmonic vibrates at twice the **base frequency**, and the fifth at five times that frequency. These whole-number multiples are **harmonics**.

teaching.text: The model of **vocal-fold vibration** predicts harmonics as well. A voice’s base frequency can differ from another’s while the whole-number relationship remains.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics

teaching.text: A string can vibrate in **several modes at once**. Adding the movement from each mode at every point gives the changing shape of the combined string.
The higher modes repeat more quickly. While the first completes one cycle, the fifth completes five in this harmonic system.
children: The spectrum has one spike for each active frequency. Its equal spike heights are deliberately set for this demonstration, rather than being a requirement for every string sound.

sections.title: A membrane combines spatial modes

teaching.text: A **membrane** extends in two directions. Its mode labels use two numbers to describe the moving regions in those directions.
children: In **(1, 1)**, the surface rises and falls as one region. In **(2, 1)** or **(1, 2)**, two regions move against each other. In **(2, 2)**, four regions alternate, and in **(3, 1)** there are three regions along one direction.

teaching.text: The combined surface adds these separate motions. Its spectrum shows the active frequencies at the marked pickup point.
children: The harmonic frequencies in this illustration are assigned teaching values. They are not the natural frequencies calculated for the pictured rectangle.

sections.title: One fixed end and one free end

teaching.text: A **fixed–free system** has a **node** at its fixed end and an **antinode** at its free end. A node stays still through the cycle, while an antinode has the greatest motion.
Its first mode runs from no motion at one end to maximum motion at the other. Higher patterns must keep both endpoint conditions.
children: The allowed frequencies are **odd multiples** of the lowest frequency, one, three, five and seven times that frequency.

teaching.text: For the same length and wave speed, this system has a lowest frequency **half** that of a string fixed at both ends. The idealized air in the vocal tract has fixed–free endpoint conditions.

sections.title: Why fixed–free frequencies are odd multiples

teaching.text: The fixed end is a **node** and the free end is an **antinode**. A **quarter-wave packet** is the part of the spatial pattern between those two kinds of location.
The first mode fits one packet. The second fits three, the third fits five, and the fourth fits seven.
children: Packets are counted along the length of the system. They are pieces of the pattern, rather than separate masses or separate times in the motion.

teaching.text: The count must stay **odd** to finish at a moving free end. Adding two packets preserves that condition, while an even count would finish at a still node.
children: Fitting more packets into the same length makes the waves shorter and their frequency higher.

sections.title: Count quarter-waves from the boundary conditions

teaching.text: Count the **quarter-wave packets** from the fixed bottom to the free top. The first mode contains one packet, the second three, the third five and the fourth seven.
Each pattern must start at a **node** and end at an **antinode**. The extra packets add still points inside while preserving motion at the free end.
children: The mode number counts allowed patterns. It does not give the multiple of the lowest frequency. The second mode has three times that frequency.

sections.title: Air in a fixed–free tube has modes

teaching.text: The air’s **mass** allows continued motion, while its **springiness** produces a restoring effect when air is squeezed. The mass-spring chain makes those two properties visible.
The fixed end represents the vocal-fold end of the tract, and the free end represents the lips. **F1** and **F2** name the first and second air resonances, or **formants**.
In this **uniform fixed–free tube**, F2 is three times F1 and F3 is five times F1.
children: The number in F2 orders the resonances from lowest to highest. It does not mean twice F1. The odd-multiple relationship describes the uniform tube, rather than every vowel shape.

teaching.text: The three marked positions locate the /a/, /i/ and /u/ constrictions. Each position can have a different role in mode 1 and mode 2.

sections.title: Compression and motion alternate in an air column

teaching.text: The **closed vocal-fold end** prevents back-and-forth air motion, while the **open lip end** allows it. These are the fixed and free ends of the model.
**Motion and compression are different.** A line can move far while keeping the same distance from its neighbors. Compression happens when those distances shrink, and expansion when they grow.
A **node** stays still, but the air beside it can move toward and away from it. Strong compression around a still point is therefore consistent with no motion at that point.
children: Mode 1 has its only motion node at the closed end. Mode 2 adds one internal node, and mode 3 adds two.

teaching.text: **F1, F2 and F3** order the air resonances from lowest to highest. Their odd-multiple relationship belongs to the uniform fixed–free model. A constriction changes the tract’s resonances.

sections.title: Vowel shape locates a constriction

teaching.text: Vowels differ in where the tongue and lips create a **constriction**, a narrowing in the vocal tract. **High/low** describes tongue height, and **front/back** describes its location along the tract.

The high front vowel in **Dean** has a narrowing near two thirds of the distance from the **glottis**, the opening between the vocal folds. The low back vowel in **Don** has a narrowing near one third.
children: **Dune** includes lip rounding and a back tongue constriction. **Done** is the central, unmarked-constriction example, while **Dan** is low and front.

teaching.text: The location matters because different parts of each mode have different amounts of motion and compression. The modeled lip constriction of **/u/** has a strong effect on the first two formants.

For **/u/**, the back tongue constriction and the lip constriction play different roles. In this account, the back constriction is the example where the effects balance and leave the formants unchanged. The lip constriction lowers the first two formants.

sections.title: Why a constriction can raise one formant and lower another

teaching.text: Narrowing the tract increases both effective **mass** and **stiffness** of the air at the constriction. More mass tends to slow vibration, while more stiffness tends to speed it up.

A location’s **motion and compression** decide which effect is stronger. Where air mostly travels back and forth, the mass increase matters most. Where it mostly compresses and expands, the stiffness increase matters most.
children: The increases act at one location, but that location can be strongly moving in one mode and strongly compressing in another.

teaching.text: This is why **one constriction can shift two formants in opposite directions**. Raising both properties is not enough information to predict cancellation.

sections.title: Compression and motion alternate in an air column

teaching.text: At each location in the air column, distinguish **movement of the air** from **change in spacing between neighboring parts**. The second is compression and expansion.
A constriction at a strongly moving location tends to **lower that mode’s formant** because of added mass. A constriction where compression is strong tends to **raise it** because of added stiffness.
children: Near the closed end, motion is weak and compression is strong. Near the open lips, motion is strong and compression is weak.

sections.title: Air in a fixed–free tube has modes

teaching.text: Both modes move strongly at the **lip end**. Inside the tube their patterns differ, so the same marked point can have strong motion in one mode and strong compression in the other.
The modeled **/a/** constriction is near one third of the distance from the glottis, and **/i/** is near two thirds. **/u/** loads the lip end.
children: For each formant, the local movement decides how much added mass matters, and local compression decides how much added stiffness matters.

sections.title: /u/ loads the moving lip end

teaching.text: **Loading the free end** means increasing effective mass near the lips. Lip rounding for **/u/** produces that change in the model.
The air moves strongly there in **both mode 1 and mode 2**. Its neighboring parts have little relative compression, so added mass matters much more than added stiffness.
Both modes slow, giving **lower F1 and lower F2**. The recorded change from schwa into /u/ shows the same downward movement of both formants.

sections.title: /i/ has opposite effects on F1 and F2

teaching.text: The **/i/** constriction is near two thirds of the distance from the glottis. Its effect depends on the pattern of each mode, not simply on narrowing the passage.
In **mode 1**, that region mostly moves. Increasing its mass slows the mode, so **F1 decreases**.
In **mode 2**, that region mostly compresses and expands. Increasing its stiffness strengthens the restoring action, so **F2 increases**.
children: A recording that changes from schwa into /i/ shows the same separation, with F1 falling and F2 rising.

sections.title: /a/ reverses the two effects

teaching.text: For **/a/**, the narrowing is near one third of the distance from the glottis. It adds effective mass and stiffness at that location.
The first mode has strong compression there, so increased stiffness raises **F1**. The second mode has strong motion there, so increased mass lowers **F2**.
children: The outcome, **F1 up and F2 down**, follows the motion and compression at the marked location. A narrowing does not push every resonance in the same direction.

sections.title: Compression and motion alternate in an air column

teaching.text: **Motion and compression alternate along the air column.** In one region, air travels strongly with little change in spacing. In another, the spacing changes strongly while local motion is small.
Higher modes place those regions differently. A constriction can therefore fall in a moving region for one formant and a compressing region for another.
children: Predict the effect separately for each mode. Added moving mass lowers its frequency, while added stiffness where air compresses raises it.

sections.title: The source supplies harmonics and the filter shapes their heights

teaching.text: A vowel combines **source** and **filter**. Vocal-fold vibration supplies the source harmonics. Air resonances in the vocal tract supply the filter formants.
The filter changes **how strongly each harmonic appears**. Harmonics near a formant become tall peaks, while those between formants remain shorter.
children: A formant is therefore visible through a group of harmonic heights. It is not simply another harmonic added between them.

teaching.text: The **envelope** is the smooth overall outline of those heights. A different vowel has different formant positions and a different envelope.
children: When the source stays the same, changing the vowel leaves the harmonics at the same frequencies and changes their amplitudes.

sections.title: The /i/ filter keeps F1 low and F2 high

teaching.text: The **/i/** filter has a **low F1** and a **high F2**. Harmonics near those resonances become strong, leaving a wide gap between the two groups of tall peaks.
The source’s harmonic frequencies stay the same. What changes is their **amplitude**, giving the envelope its /i/ pattern.
children: The widely separated formants agree with the modeled /i/ constriction, which lowers F1 and raises F2.

sections.title: The /a/ filter raises F1 and lowers F2

teaching.text: The **/a/** filter has a **higher F1** and a **lower F2**, placing the first two formants closer together. Harmonics near them become tall and form a broad low-frequency group.
The harmonics remain at the frequencies supplied by the source. The filter changes their **heights**, creating the envelope for /a/.
children: The formant positions agree with the modeled constriction that raises F1 and lowers F2.

sections.title: A spectrogram places successive spectra in time

teaching.text: A **spectrogram** follows sound through time. It combines many short spectra, rather than showing only one moment.
Read **time horizontally** and **frequency vertically**. **Amplitude becomes darkness**, so a tall peak in a spectrum becomes a dark region at its frequency.
A **formant band** marks a region of strong harmonic energy around an air resonance. Following the band tracks how that resonance changes as the tract changes shape.
children: The /i/ portion has low F1 and high F2. In the /a/ portion the first band rises and the second falls, so they become closer together.

sections.title: Reflection prompt
Wide harmonic spacing makes formants harder to identify

teaching.text: A **formant** is an air resonance, while a **harmonic** is a multiple of the vocal-fold base frequency. A formant strengthens nearby harmonics, so their heights reveal its position.
With low **F0**, many closely spaced harmonics trace each formant region. Raising F0 spreads the harmonics apart and leaves fewer peaks to show the same filter.
children: A formant can fall between widely spaced harmonics. The difficulty is then seeing the resonance from a few peaks, rather than the formant disappearing.

teaching.text: High-pitched voices can therefore make formants hard to locate. The harmonic spacing changes with F0 even if the **vocal-tract filter stays fixed**.

sections.title: Homework 4 lab reminder
Speech → Neural Networks
Five membrane modes combine into one motion

teaching.text: The **vocal folds** form a vibrating membrane. A **mode** is a pattern of movement across that whole membrane.
children: In **mode 1**, the membrane moves together. In **mode 2**, one region moves up while another moves down. Higher modes divide the surface into more regions moving against one another.
Several modes can occur at the same time. Their movements add together to produce one combined motion.

teaching.text: The illustrated source has **harmonics**, frequencies at whole-number multiples of the lowest frequency. That lowest frequency is **F0**, the fundamental frequency.
children: A spectrum separates the combined motion into its frequencies. Each spike identifies one contribution; the combined surface does not have to move in just one mode.

sections.title: A fixed end and a free end select odd harmonics

teaching.text: A **fixed–free system** has a fixed end that stays still and a free end that moves. Every allowed mode must fit both conditions.
children: The fixed end is a **node**, a point with no displacement during the cycle. The free end is an **antinode**, where the movement is largest.

teaching.text: These end conditions allow the **odd harmonics**, at one, three, five and seven times the lowest frequency. The second allowed mode is therefore three times the lowest frequency, rather than twice it.
For the same length and wave speed, freeing one end lowers the first mode to half the frequency of the fixed–fixed system.

sections.title: Quarter-wavelength packets explain the allowed modes

teaching.text: A **quarter-wave packet** runs from a node to an antinode. One packet fits the first mode of a fixed–free system because the pattern starts still and ends moving.
Mode 2 fits **three packets** in the same length. Modes 3 and 4 fit five and seven. More packets mean a shorter wavelength and a higher frequency.
children: An even number of packets would finish at a node. That would violate the moving condition at the free end, so the allowed counts are odd.
The packets describe parts of one standing pattern, rather than separate objects traveling along the system.

sections.title: Air moves longitudinally in vocal-tract modes

teaching.text: The **air in the vocal tract** is a second vibrating system, separate from the vocal folds. Its movement is **longitudinal**, back and forth along the length of the tract.
In the neutral-tube model, the vocal-fold end is **closed** and the lip end is **open**. Air next to the closed end cannot move back and forth there; air at the lips can.
children: The air can be modeled as a chain of masses joined by springs. The mass describes the air that moves, and the spring describes its compression and expansion.

teaching.text: The air’s resonant frequencies are **formants**. **F1** is the first resonance and **F2** is the second. For a uniform fixed–free tube, their frequencies follow the odd-multiple pattern.
children: The marked locations identify the vowel models: /a/ near one third of the distance from the closed end, /i/ near two thirds, and /u/ at the lips.

sections.title: Track air motion separately from compression

teaching.text: Air can **move back and forth** while neighboring portions stay nearly the same distance apart. That is strong movement with little compression.
Air can also **compress and expand** as neighboring portions approach and separate. This changing spacing supplies the restoring effect called **springiness**.
children: Near the closed end, the air has little movement but strong compression and expansion. At the open end, the air moves strongly with little compression.

teaching.text: In **mode 1**, motion becomes stronger toward the open end while springiness becomes weaker. Higher modes alternate between regions of strong motion and regions of strong compression more times along the tract.

sections.title: Compare positions within an air mode

teaching.text: At each marked position, ask whether the air mainly **travels together** or **compresses and expands**. The answer comes from the movement throughout the cycle, rather than the air’s position in one still frame.
children: A region where the slices approach and separate strongly is springy. A region where they travel together with little change in spacing mainly shows the moving mass.

teaching.text: A **constriction** increases both the effective mass and the stiffness of the air. Its effect depends on the mode’s behavior at that location.
children: Where compression is strong and movement is small, the stiffness increase matters more, so the formant rises.
Where movement is strong and compression is small, the mass increase matters more, so the formant falls.

sections.title: Vowel positions change where the tract is narrowed

teaching.text: A **constriction** is a narrowing of the vocal tract. The MRI images show that different vowels place this narrowing in different locations.
children: For **/i/** in dean, the tongue is high and forward, narrowing the tract near two thirds of the distance from the glottis.
For **/u/** in dune, the model emphasizes the narrowing at the lips. For **/a/** in Don, it emphasizes a narrowing farther back, near one third of the distance from the glottis.
The central vowel in done is the neutral comparison, with no marked constriction in this model. Dan has a low, front tongue position.

teaching.text: The location matters because **each air mode has its own pattern of motion and compression**. The same narrowing can therefore affect F1 and F2 differently.

sections.title: A constriction changes inertia and restoring stiffness

teaching.text: Narrowing the tract increases the air’s **effective mass** and **stiffness** at that location. More mass tends to lower a frequency; more stiffness tends to raise it.
The two changes do not automatically cancel. A mode has its greatest movement in different places from its greatest compression.
children: At a strongly moving location, the added mass has the larger effect, so the formant falls.
At a strongly compressing location, the added stiffness has the larger effect, so the formant rises.

teaching.text: The prediction must be made **for each mode separately**. A location that mainly moves in mode 1 can mainly compress in mode 2, giving opposite changes in F1 and F2.

sections.title: Use both modes to interpret the same tract location

teaching.text: Compare **mode 1 and mode 2 at the same location**. Each is a pattern for the whole air column, and each uses that location differently.
children: At the lips, both modes have strong air movement. Inside the tract, one mode can have strong movement where the other has strong compression.
A constriction changes F1 according to mode 1’s behavior there, and changes F2 according to mode 2’s behavior there. F1 and F2 are resonances of the air, separate from the vocal-fold harmonics.

sections.title: Lip loading lowers both F1 and F2 in the /u/ model

teaching.text: For **/u/**, narrowing at the lips **loads the free end**. Loading means adding effective mass at the part of the air column that moves strongly.
Both mode 1 and mode 2 have strong movement at the lips, with little compression. The increased mass therefore has the larger effect in both modes, giving **F1 down and F2 down**.
children: The constriction also increases stiffness, but that increase matters little where compression is small.
The low formants in vowels such as dune are consistent with this prediction.

sections.title: A front constriction separates the effects on F1 and F2

teaching.text: For **/i/**, the constriction is near **two thirds of the distance from the closed end**. The air behaves differently there in the first two modes.
children: In **mode 1**, the air mainly moves back and forth. The increase in effective mass dominates, so **F1 falls**.
In **mode 2**, the air mainly compresses and expands. The increase in stiffness dominates, so **F2 rises**.

teaching.text: The resulting /i/ pattern is **low F1 and high F2**. A transition from the neutral vowel into /i/ therefore moves the first formant downward and the second upward.

sections.title: A back constriction reverses the F1 and F2 pattern

teaching.text: For **/a/**, the constriction is farther back, near **one third of the distance from the closed end**.
children: In **mode 1**, strong compression makes the increase in stiffness matter more, so **F1 rises**.
In **mode 2**, strong movement makes the increase in effective mass matter more, so **F2 falls**.

teaching.text: The first two formants move closer together. This reverses the /i/ pattern, because the constriction is acting at a different location in the two mode patterns.

sections.title: Air motion and compression in the vocal-tract modes

teaching.text: **Motion** describes how far a portion of air moves back and forth. **Compression** describes how much the distance between neighboring portions changes.
children: Neighboring portions can move far together and remain evenly spaced. Elsewhere, their individual movement can be small while the distance between them changes strongly.

teaching.text: The first three modes alternate between these behaviors at different places. To predict a constriction’s effect, follow the relevant mode and check **movement and changing spacing at the constriction**.

sections.title: The vocal-fold source sets harmonic spacing

teaching.text: The **vocal-fold source** supplies harmonics. **F0**, its lowest frequency, also sets the spacing between those harmonics.
children: A low F0 puts the harmonics close together. A high F0 places them farther apart.
Greater vocal-fold mass and lower stiffness favor a lower F0. Lower mass and greater stiffness favor a higher F0.

teaching.text: Changes in **F0 over time** contribute to intonation. The same words, “the dog slept here,” can sound like a statement or a question when their pitch pattern changes.
children: The pitch change comes from the **vocal-fold source**. The vowel’s formant pattern comes from the **air in the vocal tract**, so changing F0 and changing a formant are different changes.

sections.title: The vocal-tract filter favors nearby harmonics

teaching.text: The **vocal tract is the filter**. Its resonances, the **formants**, make source harmonics near those frequencies stronger and harmonics farther away weaker.
children: A harmonic near a formant becomes stronger **at its own frequency**. A formant does not move a harmonic onto the formant frequency; it makes nearby available harmonics more prominent.

teaching.text: For the neutral uniform tube, the formants follow the odd-multiple pattern. Constrictions change that pattern.
children: **/u/** has low F1 and low F2. **/i/** has low F1 and high F2. **/a/** has a higher F1 and a lower F2 than the neutral comparison.

teaching.text: The source supplies the harmonic frequencies, while the filter shapes **their relative strengths**. The resulting spectrum contains both influences.

sections.title: One filter can look different at different pitches

teaching.text: The **same vowel filter** can produce different-looking spectra when **F0** changes. F0 determines how many source harmonics fall near the formants.
children: With a low F0, many closely spaced harmonics show the rises and falls of the filter clearly.
With a high F0, the widely spaced harmonics can leave few or no harmonics near a formant. The vowel pattern then becomes harder to identify from the spectrum.

A **formant can still exist even if the sparse harmonics do not show it clearly**. The resonance belongs to the air in the tract; the source determines which harmonic frequencies are available to reveal it.

teaching.text: A spectral slice can be used to identify the source harmonics and measure F0. The lowest harmonic gives the fundamental, and the others occur at its multiples.

sections.title: Map spectra into a spectrogram

teaching.text: A **spectrum** shows frequency and amplitude at one moment. A **spectrogram** shows how that information changes over time.
children: In a spectrogram, time runs from left to right, frequency runs from low to high, and darker regions indicate greater amplitude.
The **height of a spectral peak becomes darkness** in the spectrogram. A taller peak at one frequency therefore contributes a darker mark at that frequency and moment.

teaching.text: The dark formant bands trace the changing vocal tract. During **/ia/**, **F1 rises and F2 falls** as the sound changes from /i/ toward /a/.

sections.title: Reflection prompt

teaching.text: Connected speech contains **changing formants**, because the vocal tract changes shape throughout a phrase.
children: In “Where were you a year ago?”, an /i/-like region has low F1 and high F2. The /u/-like sound in you brings the formants down.
The rises and falls of the bands record the changes from one sound to another, rather than a sequence of completely steady vowels.

sections.title: Speech-complexity experiment prompt

teaching.text: A speech-perception experiment joins **the consonant from ma** to **the vowel from na**. Listeners hear **na**, even though the initial consonant was taken from ma.
The vowel contains information about the consonant. The vowel after n has a strong formant transition that differs from the more stationary pattern after m.
children: That transition in the vowel can outweigh the information in the isolated consonant segment.

teaching.text: **Speech perception uses a stretch of sound over time.** The decision about a consonant can depend on acoustic information in the following vowel.

sections.title: Use formants as input to vowel recognition

teaching.text: A **neural network** can use **F1 and F2** to recognize a vowel. The formants are the input numbers, and the output is a decision about which vowel produced them.
children: **Weights**, often written W, are the numbers that control how the network uses its inputs. Training changes these weights so that the network’s decisions better match the known vowels.

sections.title: A fully connected linear vowel network

teaching.text: A **fully connected network** connects every neuron in one layer to every neuron in the next. This one receives two formants, processes them through hidden layers, and has five output neurons.
children: The two inputs are **F1 and F2**. The five outputs represent the vowels in done, dune, dean, Don and Dan.
One pair of formants leads to **one decision among five vowel alternatives**. The output neurons describe competing answers for the same recording, rather than five different recordings.

teaching.text: Each hidden neuron takes an **inner product**, also called a **weighted sum**. It multiplies each incoming value by its connection weight, then adds the products.
children: This is a **linear network**, with no activation function between layers. Each layer’s results become the next layer’s inputs.

sections.title: Random weights assign signed contributions to connections

teaching.text: A **weight** controls how strongly an input contributes to a neuron. For a positive input, a positive weight adds to the next neuron’s value, and a negative weight subtracts from it.
children: The size of the weight controls the size of that contribution. The blue and orange connections distinguish positive and negative weights.

teaching.text: Before training, the weights are **random**, so they do not yet contain useful knowledge about the vowels. A low F1 and high F2 identify an /i/-like input, but random weights can still lead to the wrong answer.

sections.title: Forward flow and an illustrative output distribution

teaching.text: In **forward propagation**, the formants pass through the network one layer at a time. Each neuron calculates a weighted sum, and those values become the inputs to the next layer.
The final scores are converted into a **probability distribution** over the five vowels. The probabilities add up to one, and the largest identifies the network’s choice.
children: Here the network favors done even though the input is /i/, as in dean. A valid probability distribution can still give the wrong answer.

teaching.text: A **target** supplies the known vowel. Training uses the difference between the prediction and the target to change the weights, so a repeated presentation of those formants can favor dean more strongly.

sections.title: Declare the layer sequence in PyTorch

teaching.text: **PyTorch** provides tools for building a neural network in Python. **nn.Sequential** puts the processing layers in the order that the inputs pass through them.
Each **nn.Linear** specifies the number of inputs and outputs for a weighted-sum layer.
children: The sequence is **2 → 3 → 2 → 4 → 5**. The first layer receives F1 and F2; the last produces a score for each of the five vowels.
Each layer’s output size matches the input size of the next layer. Setting **bias=False** removes the bias, an extra constant that would otherwise be added to a weighted sum.

teaching.text: Declaring this structure **does not train it**. Training also requires examples, their correct answers, and instructions for adjusting the weights.

lecture15.title: Neural Networks · Forward propagation, learning, and sigmoid

sections.title: Neural Networks
Two formants feed a fully connected network

teaching.text: A **neural network** takes numbers as input and processes them to make a decision. Here **F1 and F2** describe a vowel, and the network chooses among done, dune, dean, Don and Dan.
children: The input neurons receive the two measurements. The **hidden layers** are the processing layers between the input and output. Each output neuron represents one vowel alternative.

teaching.text: The network is **fully connected**, so every neuron connects to every neuron in the next layer. Each connection has a **weight**, a number that controls its contribution.
children: The **input values describe one recording**, while the **weights control how recordings are processed**. A new recording changes F1 and F2; learning changes the weights.
The weights hold the network’s learned knowledge. Their signs and sizes determine how the incoming values combine in a weighted sum.

sections.title: Forward propagation combines weighted inputs

teaching.text: **Forward propagation** carries the input through the layers to produce an answer. Each neuron calculates an **inner product**, multiplying incoming values by their weights and adding the products.
children: For the marked first-layer neuron, the F1 contribution is positive and the F2 contribution is negative. Their combined effect produces the neuron’s **activation**, its current output value.

teaching.text: One layer’s activations become the next layer’s inputs. The same weighted-sum operation continues until the output layer has a score for each vowel.
**Softmax** converts the final scores into a **probability distribution**. The probabilities add up to one, and a larger score gives a larger probability.
children: **Adding up to one does not make a prediction correct.** Correctness depends on whether the favored vowel matches the vowel that actually produced the recording.
The example gives the highest probability to done, so done is the network’s decision. Making a decision with the learned weights is called **inference**.

sections.title: Pop quiz · Forward propagation
Info on Exam 2 and Exam 3
Backpropagation uses the difference between prediction and target

teaching.text: The **computed output** is the network’s prediction. The **desired output**, or **target**, specifies the vowel that actually produced the formants.
children: A **one-hot target** has a one for the correct vowel and zeros for the other vowels. For dean, only the dean position is one.
The **target comes from the known recording label**. Learning changes the weights to approach that answer; it does not change the target to agree with the prediction.

teaching.text: The **error**, measured by the **loss**, is the mismatch between prediction and target. The example favors done when the target is dean, so learning should increase the support for dean and reduce the support for the wrong answers.

**Backpropagation** works from the output toward the input to calculate how the error depends on the weights. **Stochastic gradient descent**, or **SGD**, uses that information to make small changes in the weights.
children: The activations from the forward pass are retained for the backward calculation. Repeated weight adjustments gradually improve how the same input is processed.

sections.title: Predict how changing a marked weight affects error

teaching.text: For the marked connection into **done**, the activation feeding it is positive and its weight is positive. Increasing that weight increases done’s score and probability.
children: Because the correct answer is dean, making done more likely increases the error. **Decreasing this marked weight** moves its contribution in the useful direction.

This direction follows from **this connection’s positive activation and its destination, done**. It is not a rule that every weight should decrease. A different sign or target can call for a different change.

teaching.text: An early weight has a less direct effect. It changes a hidden activation, which changes later activations before the output probabilities change.
children: Those later calculations involve many positive and negative weights. The effect cannot be decided from the early weight alone; the backward calculation accounts for the path to the error.

sections.title: Backpropagation reuses downstream error calculations

teaching.text: **Backpropagation starts at the output** because the last weights have the most direct connection to the error. The output probabilities depend on those weights immediately.
The effect of an early weight is more involved. Changing it affects several later layers, so its contribution to the error **includes the effects of the later weights**.
children: Working backward makes the error information from those later calculations available when the earlier weights are considered.

teaching.text: This is **dynamic programming**: solve the smaller dependent problems and reuse their results to solve the larger ones. **SGD** supplies the small weight adjustments; dynamic programming explains the backward order of the calculation.

sections.title: Pair each recording with its target row

teaching.text: Training uses two **matrices**, or tables of numbers, with one row for each recording.
children: The input table has two columns, **F1 and F2**. The target table has five columns, one for each vowel. Each target row identifies the true vowel with a one and gives the other vowels zeros.
A zero in a **one-hot target** means that vowel is not the answer for this recording. It does not mean the recording or its measurement is missing.

teaching.text: The rows must **stay matched across the tables**. A pair of formants from dean must be paired with the dean target.
children: Training compares the computed output with this fixed target and changes the weights. Reordering only one table would pair recordings with the wrong answers.

sections.title: Read one full-batch training step in PyTorch

teaching.text: The **import** commands make the PyTorch library available. The **load** commands read the saved input and target tables, so the program has measurements and correct answers to work with.
**nn.Sequential** describes the order of the layers. **nn.Linear** describes a layer that combines incoming numbers through weighted sums.
children: The processing sizes are **2 → 3 → 2 → 4 → 5**. Four Linear instructions process the input through three hidden layers and into five output scores.
The two input neurons only receive F1 and F2. They do not require a separate Linear instruction.

teaching.text: The learning commands compare the prediction with the target and adjust the weights.
children: **SGD** chooses the update method, and **lr** is the learning rate, which controls the step size. **zero_grad** clears the previous stored weight-change information.
**CrossEntropyLoss** measures the mismatch. **backward** calculates how the loss depends on the weights. **step** applies the weight changes.
The **backward** calculation belongs to learning. An ordinary prediction still processes the inputs forward through the layers; it does not update the weights.

teaching.text: This program takes **one training step using all rows together**. Declaring a network, calculating its loss, and updating its weights are distinct operations.

sections.title: Sigmoid turns an inner product into a bounded activation

teaching.text: An **activation function** changes a neuron’s weighted sum into the value that it passes on. The **sigmoid** is an S-shaped activation function with outputs between zero and one.
A large negative weighted sum gives an output near zero. A large positive sum gives an output near one.
children: Near the middle of the curve, a small input change can make a substantial output change. At the flatter ends, even a larger input change has little effect.

teaching.text: The biological motivation is the near **on-or-off** behavior associated with neurons and Adrian’s work. Sigmoid gives an artificial neuron a bounded response, while still allowing values between the two ends.

sections.title: Apply sigmoid while recalculating downstream activity

teaching.text: Applying **sigmoid** changes the activation rule while keeping the input and weights fixed. Each selected hidden neuron transforms its weighted sum into a value between zero and one.
A changed activation becomes a changed input to the next layer. **All later activations must therefore be recalculated**, using the updated values rather than the old linear results.
children: The output still uses softmax, so its five probabilities continue to add up to one.

teaching.text: The preferred vowel changes as the sigmoid is applied across the hidden neurons. With all hidden neurons using sigmoid, Dan has the largest probability, so the decision still differs from the dean target.
children: This change is **not learning**. The weights have not been adjusted; the processing rule has changed.

sections.title: Insert sigmoid after the hidden linear layers

teaching.text: Adding **nn.Sigmoid** after a hidden **nn.Linear** applies sigmoid to that layer’s weighted sums. Each hidden layer still outputs the same number of values, so the network’s sizes remain **2 → 3 → 2 → 4 → 5**.
The hidden sigmoid and the final softmax have different jobs.
children: **Sigmoid** transforms each hidden neuron’s value separately into a value between zero and one.

**Softmax** treats the five final scores together to form probabilities that add up to one. The final Linear layer supplies scores to the cross-entropy loss, which handles the probability-related calculation.

teaching.text: Other activation functions, including **ReLU**, can be tested in place of sigmoid to examine how the choice affects vowel recognition.

lecture16.title: Neural Networks · Vowel data, training runs, and initialization

sections.title: Neural Networks
Two formants feed a fully connected network

teaching.text: This **fully connected neural network** receives **F1 and F2** and chooses among five vowel categories. Every neuron connects to every neuron in the next layer.
children: Input neurons receive the measurements. Hidden layers process them. The five output neurons represent done, dune, dean, Don and Dan.

teaching.text: Each connection has a **weight** that controls how the incoming value contributes to a weighted sum. The weights hold the learned information used for recognition.
children: Random initial weights have not yet learned the vowel patterns. Training compares the network’s answer with a known target and changes the weights to reduce the mismatch.

sections.title: Forward propagation combines weighted inputs

teaching.text: **Forward propagation** sends the input through the processing layers. Each neuron calculates an **inner product**, multiplying incoming values by their weights and adding the products.
children: The marked neuron combines a positive F1 contribution with a negative F2 contribution. Its **activation** is the resulting value, which becomes an input to the next layer.

teaching.text: The final scores go through **softmax** to become a **probability distribution** over the five vowels. The probabilities add up to one; the largest gives the network’s choice.
children: Here the network selects done, although the low F1 and high F2 belong to /i/, as in dean. The prediction and the known answer therefore differ.

sections.title: Pop quiz · Forward propagation
Vowel formants overlap across five categories

teaching.text: The vowel plot places **F1 on the horizontal axis** and **F2 on the vertical axis**. Each point is one recording, and its color identifies the vowel.
Each category forms a **cloud of points** because speakers and recordings vary. Dean tends toward low F1 and high F2, while Dan extends toward higher F1.
The clouds **overlap**, especially among dune, Don and done. A pair of formants in an overlapping region can fit more than one vowel category.
children: If two differently labeled recordings have **the same input pair**, changing the weights cannot give that pair two uniquely identifiable answers. The overlap limits what these two inputs alone can reveal.
Training can improve recognition, but F1 and F2 do not always provide enough information to separate the vowels perfectly. Some measurement errors also remain in the data.

sections.title: Info on Exam 2 and Exam 3
Backpropagation uses the difference between prediction and target

teaching.text: The **computed output** is the network’s prediction. The **desired output** is the known vowel, written as a **one-hot target** with one for dean and zeros for the other alternatives.
The **loss** measures the mismatch between those outputs. Learning should make dean more likely and the incorrect alternatives less likely.

**Backpropagation** calculates how the loss depends on the weights, working from the output back toward the input. **SGD**, or stochastic gradient descent, uses that calculation to adjust the weights in small steps.
children: The saved forward-pass activations are reused in this backward calculation. A new forward pass with the changed weights can then produce a different prediction.

sections.title: Predict how changing a marked weight affects error

teaching.text: The marked final connection feeds a **positive activation into done** through a positive weight. Increasing that weight raises done’s contribution to the output.
children: Because dean is the target, raising done’s probability makes the error worse. Decreasing this marked weight is the useful direction.

teaching.text: The marked early weight affects the answer through several intervening layers. Its change alters hidden activations, which combine with other weights before the probabilities change.
children: The effect depends on that whole chain. An early weight’s sign alone does not reveal which adjustment will reduce the final error.

sections.title: Backpropagation reuses downstream error calculations

teaching.text: The last weights have the **most direct effect on the output error**. Early weights affect that error through the layers between them and the output.

**Dynamic programming** reuses the results of smaller dependent calculations. In backpropagation, calculating the output-side error first provides the information needed to calculate the influence of earlier weights.
children: The earlier-weight calculation includes the later-weight effects, so the backward order avoids solving those later effects again from scratch.

teaching.text: The two learning ideas play different roles. **SGD** makes gradual weight adjustments; **dynamic programming** organizes the backward calculation that determines those adjustments.

sections.title: Pair each recording with its target row

teaching.text: Two **matrices**, or tables of numbers, pair every recording with its known answer. The input row contains **F1 and F2**; the matching target row identifies the vowel.
children: A **one-hot target** gives the correct vowel a one and the four other vowels zeros. The rows of the two tables must remain aligned.

teaching.text: Learning compares the computed output with the target and changes the weights. The target remains fixed, because it records the vowel that was actually produced.
children: A confident correct output leaves little error to correct. However, a correct choice on some examples does not by itself establish that the network has learned the general pattern.

sections.title: Read one full-batch training step in PyTorch

teaching.text: The PyTorch **import** commands provide the neural-network tools, and the **load** commands read the formant and target tables.
**Sequential** orders the layers. Each **Linear** instruction specifies a processing layer that takes weighted sums of its inputs.
children: Counting the input layer gives **five layers in the diagram**, but there are **four Linear instructions**. The difference is that receiving F1 and F2 is not a weighted-sum processing step.
The sizes **2 → 3 → 2 → 4 → 5** carry two formants through the hidden layers to five vowel scores. The input neurons receive values without a separate processing instruction.

teaching.text: **SGD** specifies the weight-update method. **lr**, the learning rate, controls how large each adjustment is.
children: A larger step can move learning faster but can be less precise. A smaller step moves more slowly.
**loss** measures the prediction’s mismatch with the target. **backward** calculates the weight influences on that loss, and **step** actually changes the weights.

teaching.text: This code uses **all rows in one update**. The saved tables supply the examples; the learning commands supply the comparison and the weight change.

sections.title: Sigmoid turns an inner product into a bounded activation

teaching.text: The **sigmoid** is an activation function that turns a weighted sum into a value between zero and one. Its curve is S-shaped.
children: A strongly negative input gives a response near zero, and a strongly positive input gives a response near one.

teaching.text: The middle of the curve is steep, so small input changes can cause substantial output changes. The ends are flatter, so even larger input changes have little effect there.
The near **on-or-off** behavior associated with biological neurons motivates this bounded activation. The artificial sigmoid still allows intermediate values rather than only exact zero or exact one.

sections.title: Apply sigmoid while recalculating downstream activity

teaching.text: Applying **sigmoid** to a hidden neuron changes the value it passes on, while the input formants and weights stay fixed.
Every later layer must use that updated value. **Recalculate the downstream weighted sums and activations** after each switch, because their inputs have changed.
children: The final output still uses softmax and remains a set of probabilities adding up to one.

teaching.text: The network’s preferred vowel changes even without a weight update. This demonstrates an **activation-function effect**, rather than learning. With every hidden neuron using sigmoid, the largest probability belongs to Dan rather than the dean target.

sections.title: Insert sigmoid after the hidden linear layers

teaching.text: The program places **nn.Sigmoid** after each hidden **nn.Linear**. Linear takes the weighted sum; Sigmoid transforms that result before the next layer receives it.
children: The number of values stays the same, so the network keeps the sizes **2 → 3 → 2 → 4 → 5**.

teaching.text: The final Linear layer supplies five scores to **CrossEntropyLoss**. The loss compares those scores with the targets and handles the softmax-related calculation.
children: The hidden sigmoid transforms each neuron separately. The final probability calculation compares the vowel alternatives together.

sections.title: One initialization · training the linear network for 2,000 updates

teaching.text: **Initialization** is the choice of starting weights. This run starts with one random initialization and repeatedly updates the same linear network on the vowel data.

The graph shows **training accuracy**, the percentage of training examples whose largest output score matches the correct vowel. The horizontal axis tracks training updates, and the vertical axis gives percent correct.
children: With **five vowel alternatives**, chance performance is about **20%**, or one correct guess in five. Knowing nothing therefore does not mean getting every answer wrong.

teaching.text: Accuracy rises and then levels off at about **45%** in this displayed run. A flat part is a **plateau**, where more updates produce little visible improvement.
children: The graph measures performance on the same examples used for training. It does not measure accuracy on a separate set of new recordings.

sections.title: Ten initializations · different paths, the same final accuracy

teaching.text: These runs keep the **data and network structure the same** and change the **random starting weights**. Each curve follows one initialization through learning.
The curves take different paths: some improve earlier, while others stay near a plateau longer. All the displayed runs eventually reach roughly the same final training accuracy.
children: A different starting point can therefore change the course of learning even when the final measured accuracy is similar.

teaching.text: The plateau stays below perfect accuracy. **Overlap among the vowel formants** helps explain why using only F1 and F2 makes perfect separation difficult.

sections.title: NNs → LLMs → Agentic Systems
Neural networks, 1943–1986 · a static vector and a few categories

teaching.text: A **vector** is a list of numbers. The vowel network takes one **static vector**, one pair of F1 and F2 measurements, and decides among a few categories.
In **parallel distributed processing**, neurons within a layer calculate responses in parallel, and information is spread across many neurons.
children: The weights determine how the numbers are processed. Backpropagation supports learning by relating errors to those weights.

The early **McCulloch and Pitts** model used the all-or-none character of neural activity. The **Parallel Distributed Processing** approach developed networks in which many neurons process and represent information together.

teaching.text: Speech and language also involve **sequences**. Formants change over time, and words arrive in an order. Modeling those patterns requires using information across moments, rather than only one fixed input vector.

sections.title: Jordan’s recurrent network for speech production

teaching.text: A **recurrent neural network** uses **feedback**: output from one moment returns through state units and affects processing at the next moment. This allows the current response to depend on recent history.
children: **Recurrent feedback is different from backpropagation.** Recurrence carries recent output into ongoing processing; backpropagation works backward from an error to calculate weight changes during learning.

teaching.text: In **Jordan’s network**, plan units specify the sequence to produce, hidden units combine information, output units produce the response, and state units carry information from recent outputs.
children: The plan and state information both feed the hidden layer. The output then updates the state, keeping the sequence going.

teaching.text: The speech-production traces show that articulatory features can extend across several sounds. Rounding, for example, can rise early and stay active through part of the sequence.

sections.title: From one neuron to agentic systems

teaching.text: A **single neuron** takes an input vector and returns one weighted sum. A **neural network** connects many neurons so that one input vector produces an output vector, such as scores for five vowels.
A **large language model**, or **LLM**, takes a sequence of vectors and predicts the next item. Each vector is a list of numbers representing an item such as a word.
children: The **context window** is the available sequence used for the prediction. Fifteen input vectors and a sixteenth-item prediction are a small example, rather than a fixed limit on the idea.
The **number of vectors** counts the items in the context. The **numbers inside a vector** describe one item. A longer context and a larger vector are different properties.
Layers of learned weights transform the input representations until the model produces probabilities for the next item.

teaching.text: For **learning**, an existing sequence supplies the correct continuation. Predicting the next word and comparing that prediction with the real word gives an error for backpropagation and **SGD** to use.
children: The **training target** is the actual next word in the sentence, rather than the model’s guess.

teaching.text: An **agentic system** connects whole LLMs with different jobs. One produces an outline, another writes a draft, a critic checks it, and a reviser changes it.
children: The critic and reviser can form a loop before the final answer is produced. **Hallucination** means producing invented information; criticism and revision aim to detect and reduce it.

teaching.text: **Inference** uses learned weights to produce an answer. **Learning** changes those weights through error-based adjustments. The prediction task requires useful knowledge about how the available information can be completed.
**Gestalt completion** uses the structure already present to supply missing information. The next-item task trains a system to supply a missing continuation from the available sequence.

sections.title: Fifteen vectors · the same next-item question for any sequence

teaching.text: A model can use **fifteen vectors to predict the sixteenth**. The important operation is predicting the next item from the available sequence; the vectors can represent several kinds of material.
children: **Fifteen is the illustrated context length**. The same next-item principle can use a much longer sequence without changing what “predict the next item” means.

teaching.text: For **words**, the sentence so far supplies the context. In “The cat that the dog chased ran up the old tree and sat on the …”, predicting a continuation requires tracking that the cat is the one that sat.

For **sound**, consecutive spectrogram frames become vectors. Predicting the next frame uses the sound over time. For **pictures**, patches are put in row-by-row order so the model can predict a missing patch.
For a **protein**, the sequence consists of amino acids. The insulin example leaves the next amino acid to be predicted.
children: Words, sound frames, picture patches and amino acids reach the model as lists of numbers. The material differs, but the next-item task remains the same.

sections.title: Which sequences can be English words?

teaching.text: **Phonotactic knowledge** is knowledge of which sound sequences a language allows. English permits a simple **consonant–vowel–consonant** syllable in words such as mat, cup and dog.
children: The pattern concerns sounds. Two letters can spell one consonant sound, as in ship, and a silent letter does not add a sound.

teaching.text: An **onset** is the consonant or consonant group before a syllable’s vowel. A **coda** is the consonant or consonant group after it.
children: English allows some consonant orders and excludes others. Flat is possible, but the starred lfat is not. Help is possible, but hepl is not. A star marks an impossible English form.

teaching.text: A word can contain several syllables, so a sequence must also be checked against the **syllable boundaries**. The t and l can occur across the boundary in At-lan-tic, although tl cannot start an English syllable.
children: The ng sound can end a syllable, as in ring, but it cannot begin one in English.

sections.title: Guessing the next letter reveals phonotactic knowledge

teaching.text: **Next-letter prediction** reveals knowledge of possible English sequences. Some beginnings allow many continuations, while others sharply restrict the next letter.
After **ra**, many letters are possible because the vowel has already arrived. After **skr**, a vowel is expected. After **sp**, l, r or a vowel can follow, while n is excluded in this onset pattern.
children: The predictions follow spelling as well as sound. After k, n is possible in a word such as knee, even though the k is silent.

teaching.text: A **probability distribution** can express these expectations. Many plausible continuations produce a broad distribution; strong constraints concentrate probability on a few choices.
children: Learning to predict the next letter requires learning the sound and spelling patterns that make those predictions accurate.

lecture18.title: Neuron, Neural Networks, LLMs and Agents

sections.title: Neuron, neural networks, LLMs and agents
From a neuron to agents that communicate

teaching.text: A **neuron** receives a vector, a list of input numbers, and calculates one **weighted sum**. A **neural network** combines many neurons and returns an output vector with a score for each possible answer.

A **large language model** processes a sequence of vectors to predict the next item. Its layers change the numerical representation of the sequence, ending in a distribution over possible continuations.

An **agentic system** connects whole language models. The outline, writing, criticism, revision and final-answer stages are different jobs, and the critic and reviser can exchange a draft more than once.
children: The models communicate through messages in human or computer languages.

teaching.text: **Inference** produces an answer using learned weights. **Learning** compares predictions with targets and adjusts those weights, using SGD and the backward calculation organized through dynamic programming.

sections.title: Parallel heads and successive layers

teaching.text: A **representation** is the information about an item carried in its vector. An LLM changes these representations through many layers to make a useful next-item prediction.
Several **heads** work in parallel within a layer. Each is a processing component with learned weights that contributes information, and the layer brings their contributions together.
children: A head is a component **inside one language model**. An agent in the outline-and-revision system is a **whole language model** assigned a job.

teaching.text: Successive layers use the representations produced by the layer before them. The result of one stage becomes the input for another, allowing the information to develop through the model.
children: **More heads** means more parallel contributions within a layer. **More layers** means more successive stages of processing. These describe the model’s width and depth, respectively.

sections.title: A dynamical rule across time and depth

teaching.text: A **dynamical system** applies a rule to its current state to produce a new state, then uses that updated state again. Its **trajectory** is the sequence of states that results.
children: For an oscillator, position and velocity are the changing state values. Repeated updates produce its back-and-forth movement.

teaching.text: A **recurrent network** carries its recent output back through state units as processing continues over time. The same learned connections are used at each time step.
In an **LLM**, the vectors change as they pass through successive layers. Depth supplies the sequence of changes: each layer uses the values produced by the preceding layer.
children: The layers have their own sets of weights. Following a value through them gives a changing path, but that path does not have to be an oscillator’s repeating curve.

teaching.text: The stock-return paths show different values developing along different trajectories. A trajectory describes how a quantity changes across the ordered stages being followed.

sections.title: One prediction task for different sequences

teaching.text: A **vector** is a list of numbers, so different kinds of material can be represented in the same general form. The model uses an ordered sequence of vectors to predict the next item.

For **words**, the preceding sentence supplies the context. In “The cat that the dog chased ran up the old tree and sat on the …”, the continuation depends on the sentence structure, including which animal sat.
For **sound**, consecutive spectrogram frames become vectors. For **pictures**, the image is divided into patches and read row by row, leaving the next patch to be predicted.
children: Sound already has a time order. A picture gains an **input order from its patch sequence**. Both can therefore supply an ordered context and a next item to predict.

teaching.text: For a **protein**, amino acids supply the sequence. The next item in the illustrated insulin sequence is **Y**.
children: The original materials differ, but each task uses the preceding vector representations to predict the following one.

sections.title: Which sequences can be English words?

teaching.text: **Phonotactic knowledge** tells which sound sequences English allows. A simple syllable can follow a **consonant–vowel–consonant** pattern, as in mat, cup and dog.
children: Sounds and letters are different. The sh in ship spells one consonant sound, and a silent final e does not add another sound.

teaching.text: The **onset** comes before the vowel, and the **coda** comes after it. English allows particular consonant orders in each position.
children: Flat and help are possible words, while the starred lfat and hepl violate the allowed order. The l is next to the vowel in both of the allowed examples.

teaching.text: **Syllable boundaries** also matter. The t and l can meet across a boundary in At-lan-tic, but tl cannot begin an English syllable.
children: The ng sound can occur at the end of a syllable, as in ring, but cannot start one in English.

sections.title: Guessing the next letter reveals phonotactic knowledge

teaching.text: Predicting the **next letter** depends on the sequence already present. Some beginnings allow many completions, while others permit only a few.
After **ra**, several consonants can follow. After **skr**, the next letter is a vowel. After **sp**, l, r or a vowel can follow, while n is excluded from that onset pattern.
children: Spelling also matters. After k, n can occur in knee, although that k does not represent a spoken sound.

teaching.text: The prediction can be expressed as a **probability distribution** over letters. A broad distribution allows many continuations; a concentrated one gives most of its probability to the few continuations that fit.
children: The model can improve only by learning regularities in the words it is trying to continue. Accurate next-letter prediction therefore reveals knowledge of English sound and spelling patterns.

Repeated **prediction and correction** can put these constraints into the weights. The training task asks for a continuation, even though succeeding at it requires knowledge about the structure of words.

sections.title: Design an agentic system for English syllables

teaching.text: A **character-level transformer** is an LLM trained to predict the next character, or letter. Existing words supply both the sequence so far and the correct next letter.
children: Training compares the prediction with the true continuation and adjusts the weights. Better predictions require learning which sound and spelling sequences English permits.

teaching.text: The small model has **four heads in each of five layers**, with **64 numbers in each token vector**. A token is an input item represented by a vector, and the vector’s **dimension** is its number of values.
children: The heads contribute within each layer. The layers transform the representations through successive processing stages.
An **attention head** consults the sequence to work out which items matter for a dependency. Predicting the continuation can require relating the current item to another item in the context.

teaching.text: Generated word examples reveal the model’s current knowledge. Early outputs can be poorly formed; more training and more words can help the output reflect English syllable patterns.
